Capital inflows into the region’s markets rebounded significantly in 2017, with gross portfolio investment inflows reaching their highest level since 2010. Valuations of various financial assets in the region also rose with the markets. Indeed, compensation for credit risk in the region narrowed further in the second half of 2017, while benchmark equity indices rose across the region. Regional currencies generally appreciated against the US dollar.

With buoyant domestic demand and improved export performance, the Hong Kong economy maintained solid growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Economic growth is expected to remain solid in 2018. Hong Kong's economic outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including monetary policy normalisation by major central banks, global financial market stability, rising protectionist sentiment and escalating geopolitical tensions. In the near term, although domestic inflationary pressures should remain moderate, certain upside risks persist. The Hong Kong economy maintained its growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product grew by 0.8% quarter on quarter in both the third and fourth quarters, similar to the average growth rate of 0.9% in the preceding two quarters (Chart 3.1). Compared with the first half of the year, private consumption continued to grow solidly and remained one of the main drivers of gross domestic product growth. Consumption growth was solid, underpinned by favourable employment and income conditions, continued optimism in consumer sentiment, and the positive wealth effect arising from higher asset prices. Although building and construction activity weakened, an increase in business capital expenditure led overall investment spending to rise markedly in the final quarter after remaining broadly stable for three quarters. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance improved further, benefiting from stronger global trade growth and the gradual recovery in inbound tourism (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net exports of goods continued to drag on gross domestic product growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to gross domestic product growth. Chart 3.1 Real gross domestic product growth and contributions from major expenditure components Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports Sustained economic growth momentum drove an increase in employment in the second half of 2017. Total employment increased by about 0.7% during the period to more than 3.85 million, with the most notable increases in construction, financing and business services, and public administration, social and personal services. As real gross domestic product growth outpaced employment growth, labour productivity showed signs of further improvement. Economic growth is expected to remain solid in 2018. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance will continue to benefit from an improved global economic growth outlook and the gradual recovery in inbound tourism. On the domestic front, private consumption is expected to continue growing, mainly on account of favourable labour market conditions. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. As regards domestic fixed capital formation, building and construction activity should grow steadily, benefiting from increased housing supply and the continued implementation of infrastructure projects. Although an improved economic environment will stimulate business capital expenditure, possible interest rate increases may have an adverse impact. The Government forecasts real gross domestic product growth of between 3% and 4% in 2018, while growth forecasts by international institutions and private-sector analysts range from 2% to 4%. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned in previous chapters, the performance of the Mainland Chinese economy amid tighter financial conditions, and developments in Hong Kong's asset markets. Domestic inflationary pressures remained contained in the second half of 2017, although sequential inflation momentum showed signs of picking up slightly in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index rose by 1.7% and 1.6% in the third and fourth quarters respectively, similar to the average increase of about 1.7% in the first half of the year. However, the three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, edged up to 2.8% in January 2018 (Chart 3.3). Prices of both tradable goods and services increased. The rebound in newly contracted private residential rents since mid-2016 may also have added to inflation momentum to some extent (Chart 3.4). In addition, labour cost pressures remained moderate over the past few quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.4 Rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index and market rents Chart 3.5 Unit labour costs and per capita wages Given that global inflation remains moderate and domestic cost increases are stable, Hong Kong's inflationary pressures are expected to remain moderate in 2018, although the underlying inflation rate may gradually rise from the eight-year low of 1.7% recorded in 2017. For example, inflationary pressures may increase in the second half of 2018 owing to the pass-through effect of growth in newly contracted private residential rents. The market consensus forecast for the headline inflation rate in 2018 is a moderate 2.2%, while the Government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. Although the inflation outlook is moderate, upside risks remain. On the external front, any larger-than-expected increase in global inflation or commodity prices could add to domestic inflation momentum. On the domestic front, the labour market has tightened further recently, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate declining from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, falling below 3% for the first time in nearly 20 years (Chart 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be close to zero, and a significant tightening of the labour market could exert additional upward pressure on inflation. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate Following the low interest-rate environment after the 2008 global financial crisis, Hong Kong households' mortgage indebtedness increased. As US dollar interest rate normalisation proceeds, Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually follow US dollar interest rates upwards, correspondingly increasing households' mortgage repayment burdens in the future and thereby weighing on household consumption. This box therefore examines the impact of an increased mortgage repayment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong. The mortgage repayment burden refers to mortgage debt-service payments (i.e. interest payments plus amortisation of loan principal) as a proportion of income. Chart B3.1 illustrates the role of the mortgage repayment burden in the transmission of interest rate shocks to private consumption. In addition to the substitution and income effects commonly cited in economic theory, and the wealth and collateral effects arising from changes in asset prices, where there is a mortgage repayment burden, interest rate shocks will also affect private consumption by changing mortgage interest payments and, in turn, households' disposable income. This impact will increase with the amount of outstanding mortgage loans. Moreover, the amount of loan principal amortisation changes with the amount of outstanding mortgage loans, which also affects private consumption by changing households' disposable income. Chart B3.1 Determinants of private consumption To measure the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption, we estimated the outstanding mortgage debt-service ratio (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage debt. Unlike the existing mortgage repayment burden measure, which applies only to newly drawn mortgage debt, the OMDSR covers all outstanding mortgage debt of the household sector, which is more closely related to aggregate private consumption. Broadly following the methodology used by the Bank for International Settlements, we measure the OMDSR using the standard formula for fixed instalment payments: where Dt is the amount of outstanding residential mortgage loans in the banking sector, Yt is the aggregate income of owner-occupier households (proxied by the median income of owner-occupier households multiplied by the number of owner-occupier households), and rt and st are respectively the average interest rate and maturity of outstanding mortgage loans. To assess whether the OMDSR reliably measures the mortgage repayment burden of the household sector as a whole, it is useful to compare the OMDSR with two commonly used debt-service burden measures. Chart B3.2 shows estimates of the OMDSR from 1985 to mid-2017, together with the median ratio of mortgage payments and loan repayments to income estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on the five-yearly Population Census. In the early 2000s, both ratios trended downwards, consistent with the decline in overall household mortgage borrowing following the bursting of the property market bubble in 1997 and the sharp fall in mortgage interest rates over the same period. Despite the sharp rise in property prices after the global financial crisis, both ratios remained stable because the HKMA's macroprudential measures on banks' mortgage lending restrained overall household mortgage leverage. In addition, the lengthening of maturities for newly drawn mortgage loans also reduced the actual amount of mortgage repayments. Chart B3.2 OMDSR and median ratio of mortgage payments and loan repayments to income We also compare the OMDSR with banks' debt-service-to-income ratio, which is the actual debt-service-to-income ratio of applicants for newly drawn mortgages at banks. As shown in Chart B3.3, the OMDSR is lower than banks' debt-service-to-income ratio, partly because the OMDSR covers not only newly drawn mortgages but also existing mortgages. As property prices were lower when existing mortgages were originated, their repayments are correspondingly lower than those on newly drawn mortgages. Therefore, the measure of the repayment burden on outstanding mortgages covering both existing and newly drawn mortgages (i.e. the OMDSR) is lower than the measure of the repayment burden on newly drawn mortgages (i.e. banks' debt-service-to-income ratio). Moreover, banks' debt-service-to-income ratio is also higher because, in compliance with the HKMA's prudential supervisory requirements, banks include repayments on non-mortgage loans when calculating the debt-service-to-income ratio. Following the global financial crisis, both the OMDSR and banks' debt-service-to-income ratio remained stable, mainly owing to the HKMA's implementation of prudential supervision of mortgage lending, which imposed a cap on banks' debt-service-to-income ratio and also helped stabilise the OMDSR. Chart B3.3 OMDSR and banks' debt-service-to-income ratio for newly drawn mortgages Overall, the OMDSR is broadly consistent with commonly used debt-service burden measures, but it is more timely and can capture the burden of all outstanding mortgage debt rather than only newly drawn mortgage debt. We therefore believe that the OMDSR can be used to assess the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption. To assess the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimate an error-correction model following the approaches of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). In the short-run equation, the long-run relationship between real private consumption (proxied by real average private consumption per household) and its determinants is represented by an error-correction term. Based on existing theoretical and empirical evidence, we use real income (proxied by median household income and deflated by the Composite Consumer Price Index), real housing and financial wealth (proxied respectively by residential property prices and the Hang Seng Index and deflated by the Composite Consumer Price Index), and the OMDSR as the long-run determinants of private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, while the local interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. Total loans continued to increase in the second half of 2017, albeit at a slower pace than in the first half. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. Volatility in fund flows may increase if global financial market sentiment changes abruptly. In the second half of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar fluctuated between 7.799 and 7.827 (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate strengthened briefly and remained near 7.80 between September and November 2017. This was mainly attributable to increased funding demand from initial public offerings and banks’ prudent approach to liquidity management ahead of month-end and year-end, which led to tighter liquidity conditions, thereby slowing interest rate arbitrage activities and increasing the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions. As tight Hong Kong dollar liquidity conditions eased and year-end commercial demand for the US dollar increased, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate weakened again in mid-December 2017. Entering 2018, despite increased volatility in global financial markets, particularly equity markets, the Hong Kong dollar continued to operate in an orderly manner. During the reporting period, the Hong Kong dollar weakened against the US dollar, but the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Fund-flow indicators The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar fluctuated slightly in the second half of 2017, but has recently faced greater downward pressure as the US dollar weakened further (Chart 4.3). This was broadly consistent with the movements of the US dollar against most major currencies. As inflation differentials between Hong Kong and its trading partners were small and had limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index, the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar continued to closely track movements in the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates Non-residents’ portfolio investment recorded inflows in the second half of 2017. The latest balance-of-payments statistics showed that equity portfolio investment by both residents and non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter, reflecting an improved regional economic outlook and optimistic market sentiment (Table 4.A). Non-residents’ debt securities investment recorded inflows in the third quarter of 2017, offsetting outflows from residents’ debt securities investment. A survey of global mutual funds also showed that, amid market optimism about the economic outlook and corporate earnings, both equity and debt investment recorded inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017. In recent weeks, the survey data showed that equity investment continued to record inflows despite corrections in global financial markets, while bond investment recorded slight outflows (Chart 4.4). Chart 4.4 Market survey of equity- and bond-related fund flows Looking ahead, as US monetary policy normalisation continues, the negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar will widen, potentially leading to increased arbitrage activities. Therefore, the possibility of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking being triggered should not be ruled out. This is a normal process under the Linked Exchange Rate System. Meanwhile, given uncertainty over the pace of US monetary policy normalisation and rapidly changing global macro-financial conditions and market sentiment, volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may increase. The HKMA will continue to fully safeguard the stability of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate in accordance with the Currency Board mechanism. Despite the Federal Reserve’s interest rate increases and continued balance-sheet reduction, Hong Kong’s monetary conditions remained accommodative in the second half of 2017 and recently. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base increased by a further 1.4% in the second half of 2017, mainly driven by growth in Certificates of Indebtedness issued for banknote issuance (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered, the Aggregate Balance and the total amount of outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes remained broadly unchanged in the second half, at approximately HK$1,226.8 billion. Of this, the Aggregate Balance decreased, while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased correspondingly. This was due to the additional issuance of Exchange Fund Bills, totalling HK$80 billion, to meet banks’ strong demand for liquidity management. Entering 2018, the Monetary Base remained stable despite corrections in the equity market. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base Meanwhile, Hong Kong dollar money supply increased further in the second half of 2017, albeit at a slower pace. Growth in the broad Hong Kong dollar money supply (HK$ M3) slowed from 8.9% in the first half to 2.5% in the second half. As the major component of HK$ M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits edged up by 2.2% in the second half (Chart 4.7). Of these, demand deposits grew more rapidly in the second half, partly because buoyant asset markets increased investment demand. An analysis of counterpart assets showed that growth in HK$ M3 was supported by strong growth in Hong Kong dollar loans on the one hand (Chart 4.6), but was dragged down by net Hong Kong dollar fund outflows from the non-bank private sector and a contraction in banks’ net foreign currency assets on the other. Chart 4.6 Changes in HK$ M3 and its counterpart assets On the other hand, growth in foreign currency deposits was mixed. Partly reflecting the depreciation of the US dollar against most major currencies, growth in US dollar deposits declined from 3.0% in the first half to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 4.7). By contrast, after declining continuously for more than two years, other foreign currency deposits rebounded significantly by 8.4% in the second half. This was mainly driven by the recent recovery in renminbi deposits. As growth in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar deposits slowed, total deposits with authorized institutions increased slightly by 3.0% in the second half, compared with 5.6% growth in the first half. For 2017 as a whole, total deposits grew moderately by 8.7%, broadly similar to 2016. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth Between September and December 2017, increased funding demand from initial public offerings and banks’ prudent approach to liquidity management ahead of month-end and year-end exerted upward pressure on Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates (Chart 4.8). Compared with six months earlier, overnight and 3-month HIBOR rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively, reaching 0.25% and 1.26% respectively in December (on a monthly average basis). The negative spreads between Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates for tenors of 1 month to 3 months also narrowed correspondingly. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upwards but flattened, broadly mirroring movements in the US dollar yield curve. In the second half, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong Government Bonds rose by 63 basis points to close at 1.52% at end-2017, while the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds rose by a smaller 33 basis points to close at 1.83% at end-2017 (Chart 4.9). Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, composite interest rate and average interest rate for new mortgages Entering 2018, the Hong Kong dollar interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. As year-end funding demand subsided, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates declined in early January. Thereafter, despite corrections in global and local equity markets, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates remained broadly stable. Overnight and 3-month HIBOR closed at 0.43% and 1.08% respectively at end-February 2018. At the retail level, although banks’ lending rates increased as HIBOR surged, banks’ funding costs generally remained low owing to the still-large deposit base. Despite intense competition in the mortgage lending business, banks’ average interest rate for new mortgages rose gradually by 36 basis points to 2.16% in December (Chart 4.9), broadly tracking the rise in 1-month HIBOR. On the other hand, although the composite interest rate, a measure of retail banks’ Hong Kong dollar funding costs, rose temporarily in October because of increased funding demand from initial public offerings, it remained soft for most of the second half and closed at 0.38% at end-December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise and other major economies may begin interest rate normalisation, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. Meanwhile, fluctuations in global market sentiment and rapidly changing macro-financial conditions may increase the volatility of fund flows. Nevertheless, the large Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base can provide a buffer and help moderate excessively rapid increases in Hong Kong dollar interest rates. In addition, banks’ prudent liquidity management and access to discounting through the Discount Window will also help contain excessive volatility in interbank interest rates. Bank credit recorded strong growth throughout 2017. Loan growth reached 10.2% in the first half before slowing to 5.3% in the second half (Chart 4.10). Growth in both loans for use in Hong Kong and loans for use outside Hong Kong slowed in the second half of 2017. Analysed by currency, supported by favourable domestic economic conditions and relatively low Hong Kong dollar funding costs, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to grow rapidly by 9.5% in the second half, while foreign currency loans edged up by only 0.1%. Of these, growth in US dollar loans slowed to 1.8%, partly because of higher US dollar funding costs. For 2017 as a whole, total loans recorded strong growth of 16.1%, compared with 6.5% in 2016. Chart 4.10 Loan growth Growth in loans for use in Hong Kong, including trade finance, declined from 9.4% in the first half to 5.6% in the second half, with mixed performance across major sectors (Chart 4.11). Growth in loans to the construction and property development and investment sectors slowed in the second half, partly because the authorities had required banks to strengthen risk management for lending to property developers since June 2017. Despite further improvements in merchandise trade and retail sales, loans for trade finance and to the transport sector recorded only relatively modest increases, while loans to the wholesale and retail sector declined. By contrast, growth in loans to financial and finance-related enterprises remained strong, partly reflecting the steady expansion of the financial services sector. Chart 4.11 Growth in domestic loans to selected sectors Household debt increased by 6.5% in the second half of 2017, compared with 5.0% in the first half. Within household debt, growth in personal loans, including credit card advances and other loans for private purposes, accelerated further to 12.4% in the second half. The strong growth in personal loans was mainly driven by borrowing by private banking and wealth management clients secured by financial assets. Growth in these loans was broadly in line with the continued growth in client assets managed by banks. The risks associated with this type of secured lending were manageable. In addition, the HKMA issued guidelines to banks on risk management for personal loans in January 2014, requiring banks to adopt prudent risk management measures, including setting limits on loan tenors and borrowers’ debt-servicing ratios. On the other hand, although residential transaction volumes increased, the loan-to-value ratio of newly approved mortgages declined, and growth in residential mortgage loans edged down to 3.8% in the second half. Overall, the ratio of household indebtedness to GDP increased from 68.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 70.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12).

Benefiting mainly from growth in net interest income, retail banks’ profitability improved in the second half of 2017 compared with the same period in 2016. Capital and liquidity positions remained sound. After strong credit growth in the first half of 2017, growth moderated in the second half, while asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Despite a significant rise in the Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rate, retail banks’ Hong Kong dollar funding costs remained low because of low retail deposit rates. Nevertheless, banks should remain vigilant against the risks of increased interest-rate volatility and potential fund outflows amid the normalisation of US monetary policy, as well as geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and the high level of household indebtedness, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality of larger-than-expected interest-rate increases. To strengthen banks’ resilience to systemic risks, Hong Kong’s countercyclical capital buffer ratio will be raised to 2.5% with effect from 1 January 2019. In the second half of 2017, retail banks’ aggregate pre-tax operating profit increased by 13.6% year on year. This was mainly attributable to a substantial increase in net interest income and a reduction in loan impairment charges, which more than offset the decline in non-interest income. However, as assets grew faster than earnings, retail banks’ return on assets edged down from 1.17% in the first half of 2017 to 1.15% in the second half. Nevertheless, the return on assets in the second half of 2017 was still higher than the 1.11% recorded in the same period of 2016 (Chart 5.1). For 2017 as a whole, retail banks’ aggregate pre-tax operating profit increased by 15.8%, while return on assets rose from 1.09% in 2016 to 1.16%. Chart 5.1 Retail banks’ profitability Retail banks’ net interest margin widened further to 1.5% in the fourth quarter of 2017 from 1.34% in the same period of 2016 (Chart 5.2). Observational evidence indicates that the improvement in the net interest margin was consistent with the increase in the average spread on Hong Kong dollar corporate loans in Hong Kong’s syndicated loan market (Chart 5.3). Chart 5.2 Retail banks’ net interest margin Chart 5.3 Average spread on Hong Kong dollar syndicated loans Since September 2017, Hong Kong interbank interest rates have risen across the board, mainly because of liquidity demand related to initial public offerings and banks’ year-end funding needs, as well as expectations of US interest-rate increases. In particular, the 3-month Hong Kong interbank interest rate reached a post-financial-crisis high of 1.31% at the end of December 2017, up 53 basis points from the end of June, although it remained low by historical standards (blue line in Chart 5.4). Entering 2018, Hong Kong interbank interest rates appeared to stabilise as banks’ year-end liquidity needs eased. Despite the recent increase in Hong Kong interbank interest rates, retail banks’ Hong Kong dollar funding costs remained stable. This was mainly attributable to low retail deposit rates during the review period. Against this background, the composite interest rate, which reflects retail banks’ average Hong Kong dollar funding costs, remained low at around 0.3% for most of the second half of 2017, only edging up recently to 0.38% at the end of December (green line in Chart 5.4). A similar pattern was seen in the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong. In the second half of 2017, banks’ average non-deposit market funding costs in Hong Kong dollars and US dollars rose by 35 basis points, while average deposit funding costs increased slightly by 12 basis points. Overall, licensed banks’ average aggregate Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs rose by 22 basis points (red line in Chart 5.5). Chart 5.4 Interest rates Chart 5.5 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks The rise in Hong Kong interbank interest rates exceeded the increase in the banking sector’s overall funding costs, which may help improve banks’ margins on assets benchmarked to Hong Kong interbank interest rates. However, this improvement may be partially offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. In particular, market information indicates that some banks have reduced the spread between their mortgage rates and benchmark rates or introduced fixed-rate mortgage terms to attract new customers. Given expectations of further US interest-rate increases this year, banks may soon face greater upward pressure on funding costs. Given intense competition in the loan market, banks’ net interest margins could come under pressure if higher funding costs cannot be passed on fully to customers. The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained well above the international minimum standard, indicating that the Hong Kong banking sector remained well capitalised. At the end of December 2017, the total capital ratio increased from 18.7% at the end of June to 19.1% (Chart 5.6), while the Tier 1 capital ratio54 also rose to 16.6%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital.55 Chart 5.6 Capitalisation of locally incorporated authorized institutions The HKMA recently published a consultation paper on proposed rules prescribing loss-absorbing capacity requirements for authorized institutions under the Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance. Although enhancing authorized institutions’ loss-absorbing capacity helps reduce the likelihood of financial crises and thereby benefits society, it inevitably entails costs. Box 5 conducts a cost-benefit assessment of the potential impact of loss-absorbing capacity requirements on Hong Kong. Our assessment indicates that implementing the loss-absorbing capacity requirements will generate net benefits for the Hong Kong economy. Measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement under Basel III, the banking sector’s liquidity position remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions increased from 144.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 155.1% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 80% applicable in 2017. Although the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions edged down from 49.7% in the second quarter of 2017 to 49.4% in the fourth quarter, it remained well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. The ample liquidity of authorized institutions indicates that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks resulting from potential fund outflows from Hong Kong. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The Net Stable Funding Ratio, one of the Basel III liquidity standards, was implemented in Hong Kong on 1 January 2018. The requirement aims to reduce banks’ medium- and long-term funding risks by requiring them to maintain adequate stable funding sources for their business activities. Specifically, category 1 institutions must maintain a Net Stable Funding Ratio of not less than 100% at all times.57 Customer deposits remained authorized institutions’ primary source of funding, reflecting the banking system’s stable funding structure. At the end of December 2017, customer deposits accounted for 56.2% of the total liabilities of all authorized institutions, broadly unchanged from six months earlier (Chart 5.8). Chart 5.8 Liability structure of all authorized institutions The Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions rose from 77.1% at the end of June 2017 to 82.7% at the end of December (Chart 5.9), reflecting faster growth in Hong Kong dollar loans and advances than in deposits during the review period. Meanwhile, as foreign-currency deposits grew faster than loans, the foreign-currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined from 65.5% at the end of June 2017 to 63.1% at the end of December. Overall, the loan-to-deposit ratio for all currencies rose from 71.4% six months earlier to 73.0%. Banks should assess the implications of the rising loan-to-deposit ratio for their liquidity management. Chart 5.9 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions Locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest-rate risk exposures remained low. We estimate that, under a hypothetical shock involving a 200-basis-point parallel rise in interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest-rate positions would be equivalent to 3.45% of their total capital base at the end of December 2017 (Chart 5.10). Nevertheless, given expectations that the Federal Reserve will continue raising interest rates and normalising its balance sheet, banks should assess the implications for their interest-rate risk management. Chart 5.10 Impact of an interest-rate shock on locally incorporated licensed banks In the second half of 2017, amid a moderate but still favourable economic environment, growth in total loans and advances of all authorized institutions slowed to 5.3% from the strong 10.2% recorded in the first half. After two years of slowing growth, total loans grew robustly by 16.1% for 2017 as a whole. The asset quality of banks’ loan portfolios remained sound and continued to improve in the second half of 2017. At the end of December 2017, the gross classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio of all authorized institutions declined to 0.67% and 0.52% respectively, from 0.84% and 0.61% respectively at the end of June. For retail banks, the gross classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio also declined to 0.54% and 0.4% respectively (Chart 5.11). However, given the rapid growth in loans for use outside Hong Kong in recent years, banks’ asset quality may be more sensitive to the external environment, and banks should therefore closely monitor their credit risks. Chart 5.11 Asset quality of retail banks Strong credit growth is expected to continue as banks have become more optimistic about credit growth in the near term. The HKMA’s December 2017 “Survey on Credit Condition Outlook” showed that 29% of surveyed authorized institutions expected loan demand to increase over the next three months, while the remaining 71% expected loan demand to remain unchanged (Table 5.A). Credit risk associated with personal loans remained low during the review period. Banks’ mortgage portfolios remained sound, with the delinquency ratio staying low at 0.03% at the end of December 2017. The average loan-to-value ratio for newly approved mortgages fell further from 50.1% in the second quarter of 2017 to 48.8% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.12). This loan-to-value ratio was well below the 64% recorded before the HKMA introduced the first round of countercyclical macroprudential measures in September 2009.

The global economy continued to grow, but growth momentum weakened as uncertainties increased amid persistent trade frictions, tighter financial conditions, and other idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds. The Federal Reserve adjusted its monetary policy stance, stressing that decisions would be “data dependent” and that “patience” was needed, leading investors to rule out the possibility of another interest rate increase. However, financial markets may become more sensitive to incoming data, especially data that may prompt monetary policy tightening, such as a rise in US inflation. In Hong Kong, although the Hong Kong dollar triggered the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March, trading in the Hong Kong dollar continued to be smooth and orderly. In the second half of 2018, growth in total loans moderated slightly, reflecting weaker credit demand amid headwinds such as the ongoing China-US trade conflict and slower global economic growth. The residential property market also cooled in the second half of 2018, with transaction volumes falling markedly and housing prices declining, before showing signs of stabilisation in early 2019. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector faces multiple headwinds arising from increased uncertainty in the external environment. If these uncertainties intensify and persist for a prolonged period, they could significantly dampen business confidence and credit demand, thereby exerting downward pressure on banks’ profitability. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should prudently assess the impact that a potential deterioration in the external environment may have on the credit risk of their related corporate lending. The global economy continued to grow in the second half of 2018. However, while the US economy grew steadily, growth momentum in other regions slowed. Among advanced economies, growth decelerated in Japan and several major euro area countries, while inflation remained subdued. Slower global trade and a marked decline in oil prices both posed cyclical headwinds to emerging market economies. In view of weakening global growth momentum, the International Monetary Fund in January lowered its global growth forecasts for 2019 and 2020 by 0.2 and 0.1 percentage points respectively from its October 2018 forecasts. As the growth outlook dimmed and trade frictions escalated, global equity markets experienced sharp volatility at the end of 2018. The US Treasury yield curve flattened to levels not seen since the global financial crisis, fuelling market concerns that the US was approaching a recession. However, US economic fundamentals remained sound, and the likelihood of a recession in the near term was low. Nevertheless, the global economic outlook remained highly uncertain. In the US, while moderate inflation gave the Federal Reserve room to pause interest rate increases, the Federal Reserve’s data-dependent policy stance also suggested that financial markets could become more sensitive to incoming data, particularly data that might prompt monetary policy tightening, such as a rise in US inflation. Meanwhile, the outcomes of trade negotiations between the US and China and between the US and the European Union remained uncertain. In the UK, it remained unclear whether a solution to avoid a “hard Brexit” could be achieved. In East Asia, financial markets stabilised as the US dollar’s appreciation slowed and the market expected the Federal Reserve to pause interest rate increases, but a deterioration in the external environment could weigh on economic growth in the region. Indeed, weakening global trade growth had already dragged on economic growth in several East Asian economies, while inflationary pressures had also eased. Although this shift could alleviate the policy dilemma faced by central banks in the region between supporting growth and containing inflation, financial imbalances such as high private-sector indebtedness in some regional economies remained severe. As detailed in Box 1 (page 16), another challenge facing East Asia was that an unexpected change in the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy could produce shocks that spill over into the sovereign bond markets of emerging market economies, including East Asian economies. In Mainland China, growth slowed further in the second half of 2018 amid greater uncertainty in the external environment and a slight moderation in domestic demand. Looking ahead, the economic outlook remained uncertain as China-US trade negotiations had yet to reach a conclusion. The marked contraction in shadow financing activities had increased the financing difficulties faced by private enterprises, particularly small firms, over the past few quarters, while weaker economic confidence could also place pressure on business activity. In this challenging economic environment, policymakers needed to continue striking a balance between stabilising the economy and preventing and controlling potential systemic risks by adopting accommodative but targeted measures, such as targeted reserve requirement ratio cuts. Meanwhile, the authorities also introduced more supply-side measures to enhance productivity growth, such as promoting competition among firms under different forms of ownership, and to provide individuals with a better social safety net. The official growth target for 2019 was also lowered from around 6.5% in 2018 to a range of 6.0–6.5%. Risk-off sentiment dominated Mainland financial markets in 2018. Banks’ asset quality also deteriorated slightly during the review period, while the leverage of listed non-financial companies edged up. However, banks’ loan impairment provisions increased further in the second half of 2018, while their exposure to off-balance-sheet wealth management products continued to decline; both developments helped protect the banking system against a potential deterioration in credit quality. Another positive development was that the leverage of listed companies in overcapacity industries—one of the main sources of banks’ credit risk—declined further in the first three quarters of 2018. Box 2 (page 32) provides an in-depth analysis of the factors driving the recent improvement in the business performance of overcapacity industries. Compared with the first half of 2018, Hong Kong’s economic activity softened in the second half. Quarter-on-quarter GDP growth stalled and year-on-year growth also slowed, dragging full-year economic growth down from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. The weakening in economic activity mainly reflected the direct or indirect adverse effects of the China-US trade conflict on consumption and exports. Slower private consumption growth may have reflected increased economic uncertainty and the negative wealth effect arising from corrections in local asset prices. On the external front, Hong Kong’s merchandise export performance also deteriorated, particularly after China and the US implemented additional tariffs in the fourth quarter. Box 3 examines more closely the impact of the China-US trade conflict on Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance and discusses the short-term outlook and related risks. Mainly because of slower global economic growth, economic growth was expected to moderate further in 2019. Amid the interaction of multiple factors, Hong Kong’s export performance was expected to remain under pressure. Domestically, private consumption was expected to continue supporting economic growth amid low unemployment and rising household income, but the outlook for overall investment spending could become more uncertain. The Government forecast real GDP growth of between 2% and 3% in 2019, while the latest growth forecasts of private-sector analysts averaged 2.3%. These forecasts were subject to the various uncertainties and risks described above. Local inflation edged up in the second half of 2018 but remained moderate. The slight increase in inflation partly reflected earlier growth in newly contracted rents for local private residential properties. Meanwhile, although the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8%, the lowest level in more than 20 years, growth in overall employment showed signs of slowing. Looking ahead, local inflationary pressures were expected to remain moderate in 2019 as domestic economic growth momentum weakened. After the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate moved away from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499, until the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered another four times in March 2019 (as of 19 March). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate appreciated in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid tighter liquidity. Entering 2019, the Hong Kong dollar depreciated against the US dollar, partly because carry-trade positions were rebuilt. Despite the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking being triggered again in March, trading in the Hong Kong dollar continued to be smooth and orderly. As a result of the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to HK$70.9 billion (as of 19 March). Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally increased in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting expectations of US interest rate increases. Compared with June 2018, the 3-month and 12-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates rose by about 30 basis points to 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December, on a monthly average basis. Entering 2019, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally declined as seasonal demand receded. The composite interest rate, which measures the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks, rose from 0.62% at the end of June 2018 to 0.83% at the end of January 2019. In view of higher funding costs, retail banks raised their best lending rates by 12.5–25.0 basis points following the increase in the target range for the US federal funds rate at the end of September. At the end of January 2019, the average interest rate on new mortgages rose in tandem with the best lending rates to about 2.45%. As uncertainties related to China-US trade frictions and Brexit negotiations persisted, volatility in fund flows could intensify. In addition, the significant negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar could stimulate arbitrage activity and lead to fund outflows. Under such circumstances, fund outflows and the possible triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking are part of the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System. Since the beginning of 2018, both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates had come under depreciation pressure amid market concerns over escalating China-US trade frictions. However, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilised in November amid optimism fuelled by the resumption of high-level trade talks between China and the US. Although China-US trade frictions persisted, they had not so far had a significant impact on funding conditions in the offshore interbank market. The overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate remained below 4% for most of 2018, while the 3-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate hovered around 4%. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half, with renminbi customer deposits growing by 5.2% in the second half of 2018. The average daily turnover of the Renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high, rising further to RMB1,010.1 billion in 2018. Despite concerns over China-US trade frictions, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business was expected to continue expanding, supported by the Mainland’s capital account opening, the development of Stock Connect and Bond Connect, and regional economic cooperation promoted under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives. The local equity market experienced roller-coaster-like swings over the past six months. At the beginning of the review period, the market fell sharply because of continued tightening of US monetary policy, substantial differences between the two sides in China-US trade negotiations, and mounting signs of weakening economic growth in the Mainland. Subsequently, as the US economic outlook weakened and became more uncertain, the Federal Reserve shifted towards a “patient” monetary policy stance. Meanwhile, during the trade-war truce, China adopted further measures to reduce its trade surplus with the US and open its market to foreign investors. Although the US brought a highly politicised legal action against a Chinese telecommunications company, both sides made conciliatory gestures, indicating their determination to reach a trade agreement. Against this backdrop, the local equity market rebounded sharply at the beginning of the year. However, considerable uncertainty remained as the two sides discussed the details of any agreement, while future developments in the US federal government’s prosecution could complicate the situation, particularly in the high-technology sector. The Hong Kong dollar debt market grew slightly last year. Yields declined, while performance improved towards the end of the year as expectations strengthened that the pace of US monetary policy normalisation would slow. As a result, fund flows into bond funds reversed in the second half and recorded a modest increase. Issuance in Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi market rebounded sharply after three consecutive years of decline. However, as Mainland companies continued to deleverage, total issuance remained below the amount of maturing debt. Looking ahead, the local debt market remained challenging, and its outlook depended on economic developments globally, particularly in the Mainland.

During the review period, the global economy continued to grow, but growth momentum weakened under the combined impact of idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds, particularly outside the United States. In view of the dimming growth outlook, the Federal Reserve adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasising that decisions would be “data dependent” and require “patience”, and no longer provided forward guidance on further interest rate increases. As the Federal Reserve’s policy stance becomes data dependent, financial markets may become more sensitive to forthcoming data releases and may perceive monetary policy as becoming more uncertain. Meanwhile, heightened uncertainty over global trade policy and increased geopolitical risks may continue to cloud the global economic outlook. In East Asia, financial markets have broadly stabilised since the end of 2018 amid signs that the US interest rate hike cycle was slowing and the US dollar was stabilising. However, the region may face a broad-based slowdown due to the deterioration in the external environment, namely the unresolved China-US trade conflict and weakening growth in advanced economies. In Mainland China, growth momentum slowed further in the second half of 2018, while uncertainty over the growth outlook increased amid the China-US trade conflict and financing difficulties faced by small enterprises. Policymakers therefore introduced more targeted measures to stabilise the economy and support private and small enterprises. In the face of these challenges, policymakers will need to strike a careful balance between continuing to prevent and control systemic risks and supporting enterprises and the real economy. In the second half of 2018, the global economy continued to grow broadly. However, while the US economy remained generally robust, some signs of moderation emerged. There were also clear signs of weakening growth momentum outside the United States. A number of country-specific shocks, including natural disasters in Japan, the implementation of new vehicle emission standards in Germany, a surge in Italian government bond yields due to the fiscal impasse with the European Union, and social unrest in France, weighed on economic activity in advanced economies (Chart 2.1). In addition, a cyclical slowdown in global import growth created headwinds for industrial production in emerging market economies (Chart 2.2). The sharp fall in oil prices in the fourth quarter also posed new challenges to commodity-exporting emerging market economies. In view of weakening growth momentum in the second half of 2018, the International Monetary Fund lowered its 2019 global growth forecast by 0.2 percentage point to 3.5% in January. Chart 2.1 Composite Purchasing Managers’ Indices of selected advanced economies Chart 2.2 Global import volume and industrial production in emerging market economies In the fourth quarter, global equity markets underwent a sharp correction due to slowing global growth momentum, heightened trade policy uncertainty, market concerns over the sustainability of US corporate earnings growth, and the Federal Reserve’s remarks that monetary policy would continue to tighten. As financial market sentiment deteriorated, the US Treasury yield curve flattened to a level not seen since the global financial crisis, prompting some market participants to worry that the United States was approaching a recession (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 Spread between 10-year and 3-month US Treasury yields and probability of a US recession Nevertheless, the likelihood of a US recession in the near term is very low. US economic fundamentals remain robust, particularly the tight labour market, which is expected to continue supporting private consumption. Meanwhile, it is estimated that the US output gap only turned positive again last year, making it less likely that economic overheating would prompt the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy substantially. However, possibly taking into account the significant tightening of financial conditions since the fourth quarter, senior Federal Reserve officials began in early January to emphasise that monetary policy would be data dependent and noted that subdued inflationary pressures allowed them to remain “patient” in determining future monetary policy adjustments. In addition, following its January meeting, the US Federal Open Market Committee ceased providing forward guidance on further interest rate increases and announced that it “would be prepared to adjust any of the details for completing balance sheet normalisation in light of economic and financial developments”. This shift triggered a rebound in global equity markets (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 S&P 500, Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) World ex USA Index and MSCI Emerging Markets Index Despite the Federal Reserve’s recent “dovish” signals, the US monetary policy outlook remains highly uncertain, depending on inflation and other developments. Inflationary pressures have so far remained subdued, giving the Federal Reserve room to proceed gradually with monetary normalisation. Inflation expectations have remained stable in recent years, supporting the view that it “can be patient” (Chart 2.5). In addition, as Federal Reserve Chair Powell noted in January, the US economic outlook faces multiple headwinds, including slowing growth outside the United States and trade policy uncertainty. In view of these developments, the Federal Reserve may need to adopt a more cautious monetary policy stance. Chart 2.5 Market-based and survey-based measures of US inflation expectations However, the tight labour market is expected to continue supporting the overall performance of the US economy. In this environment, wage growth may accelerate, which typically implies higher inflation ahead (Chart 2.6). Therefore, market expectations that essentially rule out the possibility of a Federal Reserve interest rate increase in 2019 may be overly optimistic (Chart 2.7). Chart 2.6 Average hourly earnings and core personal consumption expenditure inflation Chart 2.7 Futures-implied probabilities of the federal funds rate target range remaining unchanged in 2019 and of at least one interest rate increase In summary, an extended pause in interest rate increases by the Federal Reserve is not a foregone conclusion. To reduce policy errors, the Federal Reserve has increasingly emphasised that its decisions will be data dependent as a risk-management strategy. It follows that financial markets may become more sensitive to forthcoming data releases, particularly data that may prompt monetary policy tightening. The monetary policies of other major central banks are also uncertain. In the euro area, the European Central Bank ended its asset purchase programme in December, while continuing to reinvest in full the principal payments from maturing securities purchased under the programme, and reiterated its forward guidance that policy rates would remain unchanged at least through the summer of 2019. However, the European Central Bank downgraded its assessment of near-term growth in January, describing risks to the growth outlook as having “moved to the downside”. The implications of this downgrade of the economic growth assessment for monetary policy remain to be seen. In Japan, the Bank of Japan stated at its latest policy meeting that it would ease its monetary policy stance if necessary amid increasing downside risks. However, the obstacles to further monetary easing may be substantial, given doubts about its effectiveness and the increasingly evident drawbacks of a prolonged ultra-low interest rate environment. For example, regional banks’ capital ratios declined from 10.6% in 2015 to 9.7% in 2018 as persistently low yields continued to weigh on profitability. The Bank of Japan therefore has very limited scope to adjust monetary policy in the near term. In addition to uncertainties surrounding the global monetary policy outlook, uncertainty over the outcomes of future trade negotiations and heightened geopolitical risks are two major sources of risk to the global economic outlook. The US government announced in early December that it would not increase tariffs on imports from China for 90 days and extended the deadline again at the end of February, but whether the two sides can reach a long-term trade agreement remains to be seen. Meanwhile, trade negotiations between the United States and the European Union have made little progress at this stage. As the outcomes of these trade negotiations remain uncertain, they may continue to cloud the global economic outlook. Policy and geopolitical risks are also prominent. In the United States, disagreements between the two parties over funding for border security led to a 35-day federal government shutdown from late December 2018 to late January 2019. Although the impact of the shutdown on economic growth should be temporary, strained relations between the Trump administration and the Democrat-controlled House of Representatives may lead to further policy impasses in the future. In the United Kingdom, risks associated with Brexit and its spillover effects rose sharply after the May government’s Brexit proposal was overwhelmingly rejected in mid-January, and whether a plan can be formulated at the last minute to avoid a disruptive “hard Brexit” remains uncertain. Elsewhere, geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, such as renewed US sanctions on Iran, may also create uncertainty for oil prices, thereby affecting the global growth outlook. In East Asia, after fluctuating repeatedly during the first three quarters of last year, financial markets broadly stabilised in the fourth quarter. The stabilisation of the US dollar since October and signs that the Federal Reserve would remain patient regarding further interest rate increases eased the currency depreciation and capital outflow pressures facing East Asian economies. Several regional currencies appreciated slightly against the US dollar in the fourth quarter, while portfolio investment flows returned to net inflows (Chart 2.8). Chart 2.8 East Asia: Currency index and capital flows Despite financial market stability, there are growing signs that the region will face a broad-based slowdown. As the China-US trade conflict weakened global trade momentum, regional export growth declined, causing real GDP growth in most East Asian economies to slow in the second half of last year. Indeed, the new export orders sub-indices of the Purchasing Managers’ Indices for several regional economies, which reflect near-term external trade performance, have fallen into contractionary territory since the fourth quarter, suggesting that near-term growth momentum may weaken further (Chart 2.9). Chart 2.9 Markit Purchasing Managers’ Index new export orders indices for East Asian economies Amid slowing growth and the recent decline in oil prices, inflationary pressures in East Asia have eased (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 East Asia: Headline inflation and oil prices As recent inflationary pressures and upward pressure on the US dollar have both been relatively moderate, East Asian central banks no longer face an urgent need to raise interest rates, alleviating the policy dilemma of balancing support for economic growth against containing inflation and capital outflows. However, as private-sector debt in some East Asian economies remains high by emerging-market standards, central banks still face the challenge of financial imbalances (Chart 2.11).

The Hong Kong economy softened in the second half of 2018, reflecting slower growth in private consumption and weaker export performance amid the US-China trade dispute. With global growth slowing, real Gross Domestic Product growth is also expected to moderate in 2019. Hong Kong’s growth outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including trade protectionism, the future direction of US monetary policy, and the performance of the Mainland economy. Local inflationary pressures should remain moderate in 2019, while the outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. Economic activity in Hong Kong softened in the second half of 2018. Specifically, economic activity failed to sustain the strong momentum of the first half, with quarter-on-quarter Gross Domestic Product growth turning slightly negative in the second half (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). On a year-on-year basis, economic growth also slowed, with growth in the fourth quarter at 1.3%, below trend growth, bringing full-year growth down from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. * Calculated on the basis of the expenditure-based and seasonally adjusted volume index of Gross Domestic Product. Chart 3.1 Real Gross Domestic Product growth and contributions from major expenditure components The weakening in economic activity was mainly attributable to consumption and exports being weighed down by the direct or indirect effects of the US-China trade conflict. Possibly due to heightened economic uncertainty and the negative wealth effect arising from adjustments in local asset prices, growth in private consumption moderated (Chart 3.1). Gross investment expenditure fell markedly amid fragile business confidence. Hong Kong’s external merchandise trade performance also deteriorated, especially after the US and China imposed additional tariffs in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as total imports decelerated faster than total exports, net trade still made a positive contribution to Gross Domestic Product in the fourth quarter. Box 3 examines Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance in greater detail and discusses its near-term outlook and associated risks. Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports As economic activity weakened, employment growth appeared to slow in the second half of 2018. Total employment rose by only 0.1% to around 3,873,000 at the end of 2018, lower than the 0.8% increase in the first half of 2018. Given weak output and employment growth, labour productivity remained broadly stable, with no sign of significant improvement. With global economic growth slowing further, Hong Kong’s economic growth is expected to moderate in 2019. Against a challenging external environment, Hong Kong’s export performance is expected to remain under pressure. On the domestic front, although the low unemployment rate and rising household income will continue to support private consumption, growth in private consumption is expected to moderate, partly reflecting weaker consumer confidence and the negative wealth effect caused by earlier adjustments in asset prices. As regards fixed capital formation, the outlook may become more uncertain. While building and construction activity is expected to continue growing steadily alongside increased housing supply, firms may become more cautious about capital investment as economic uncertainty rises. Business sentiment indicators such as the Hong Kong Purchasing Managers’ Index continued to hover in contractionary territory, and projections of future economic growth based on the index indicate that year-on-year Gross Domestic Product growth will slow further in the near term. The Government forecasts real Gross Domestic Product growth of between 2 and 3% in 2019, while the latest growth forecasts by private-sector analysts range from 1.5 to 2.7%. Hong Kong’s growth outlook is subject to the various uncertainties and risks discussed in the preceding two chapters. Although local inflationary pressures continued to build in recent months, they remained moderate. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index rose by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters of 2018 respectively, higher than the average increase of 2.4% in the first half of the year. The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also picked up recently, from 2.5% in July 2018 to 2.6% in January 2019 (Chart 3.3). The slight increase in inflation momentum was driven by rises in certain service prices. Earlier growth in newly signed private residential rents and faster increases in the prices of meals bought away from home continued to push up services inflation (Chart 3.4). However, labour cost pressures remained broadly moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Different indicators of consumer price inflation Chart 3.4 Rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index and market rents Chart 3.5 Unit labour costs and salary per head Looking ahead, local inflationary pressures should remain moderate in 2019. This mainly reflects weaker domestic growth momentum. However, earlier increases in private residential rents will continue to feed through to consumer price inflation. The market consensus forecast for the full-year headline inflation rate is a moderate 2.2%, while the Government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. The above inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. As for downside risks, the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate remained at around 2.8%, its lowest level in more than 20 years (Chart 3.6). If the labour market deteriorates unexpectedly, the current near-zero output gap would turn negative, potentially exerting additional downward pressure on inflation. On the other hand, if an easing of US-China trade frictions leads the local economy to outperform expectations, local inflation could be pushed higher. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate The US-China trade conflict gradually intensified in the second half of 2018: on 6 July and 23 August, the US imposed additional tariffs of 25% on US$34 billion and US$16 billion worth of imports from Mainland China respectively. Immediately following these two measures, Mainland China responded by imposing additional tariffs of 25% on an equivalent value of US goods. The US raised the stakes again on 24 September by imposing additional tariffs of 10% on US$200 billion worth of imports from Mainland China. Mainland China responded immediately by imposing additional tariffs of 5 to 10% on US$60 billion worth of US goods. The two countries subsequently began negotiations to avoid further tariff increases. As Hong Kong has traditionally served as an entrepôt between these two economies, the additional tariffs will inevitably have a direct impact on Hong Kong through the trade channel. The US-China trade dispute therefore has important implications for Hong Kong’s macroeconomic and financial stability. This box reviews Hong Kong’s recent merchandise trade performance and discusses its near-term outlook. We also attempt to use more granular data to identify traded goods directly affected by the additional tariffs, thereby examining the impact of the tariffs in greater detail. To analyse the impact of the tariffs, we first extracted data on six groups of Hong Kong re-exports affected respectively by the successive rounds of additional tariffs described in the preceding section. In the first two rounds of tariff increases, the US mainly imposed tariffs on capital goods and semi-manufactures, while Mainland China mainly targeted agricultural products, chemicals, medical equipment, and energy equipment. In the third round, the range of affected goods was broadened to include more consumer goods. For simplicity, we refer to the goods affected by these three rounds of additional tariffs as List 1, List 2, and List 3 respectively. After collecting these more granular trade data, we focused on year-on-year changes in the value of Hong Kong’s re-exports to adjust for the effects of seasonality. In addition, caution is warranted when analysing the data for September 2018, as trade activity during the month was disrupted to some extent by Super Typhoon Mangkhut. Overall, the findings in this section should be regarded only as preliminary evidence of the impact of the additional tariffs. Hong Kong re-exports of Mainland origin affected by tariffs Shortly after the additional tariffs were imposed, the relevant goods re-exported from Mainland China through Hong Kong to the US appeared to decline sharply or register slower growth (Chart B3.1). For example, growth in re-exports of List 1 and List 2 slowed in the first month after the additional tariffs were imposed, while re-exports of List 3 recorded negative growth. Moreover, re-exports of all three lists recorded negative growth in December. Chart B3.1 Value of goods re-exported from Mainland China through Hong Kong to the US in 2018 Hong Kong re-exports of US origin affected by tariffs By contrast, goods re-exported from the US through Hong Kong to Mainland China showed mixed performance (Chart B3.2). Re-exports of List 1 appeared to decline sharply in the months following the imposition of additional tariffs, but recovered towards the end of the year. Re-exports of List 2 recorded broadly negative growth throughout the year, while growth in List 3 appeared broadly stable. Chart B3.2 Value of goods re-exported from the US through Hong Kong to Mainland China in 2018 Front-loading As there is sometimes a time lag between the announcement and eventual implementation of tariffs (or simply because of the threat of additional tariffs), firms may increase shipments of affected goods ahead of the expected effective date of the tariffs. Indeed, some data and news reports indicate that such front-loading behaviour was quite widespread. Some private-sector analysts also considered this behaviour to be partly responsible for the strong overall trade figures before the tariff increases. More granular trade data showed some signs of front-loading for goods on certain tariff lists, but this appeared to involve only goods re-exported from Mainland China to the US (Chart B3.1). Growth rates for re-exports of List 1 and List 2 both increased in the months before their respective tariffs took effect. On the other hand, the growth rates of goods re-exported from the US through Hong Kong to Mainland China (Chart B3.2) showed no obvious front-loading behaviour by firms. Hong Kong re-exports unaffected by additional tariffs It is worth noting that Hong Kong re-exports directly affected by the additional tariffs accounted for only around 4 to 5% of the total value of Hong Kong’s re-exports. To gain a more complete understanding of Hong Kong’s trade performance, re-exports unaffected by the additional tariffs should also be examined. We found that re-exports unaffected by the additional tariffs recorded negative growth in each of the last two months of 2018 (Chart B3.3). In addition, the decline in growth of tariff-affected re-exports (red line) was markedly larger from the third quarter onwards, reflecting the significant impact of the tariffs. The slowdown in growth of re-exports unaffected by the additional tariffs partly reflected a broader weakening in external demand. As continuing trade frictions heighten uncertainty, global financial conditions tighten, and geopolitical risks increase, external demand may come under more widespread pressure. In particular, the trade conflict has weighed on global economic sentiment and activity, as reflected in adjustments in major stock markets. Import demand in other economies has consequently been dampened, constraining Hong Kong’s external trade performance. Chart B3.3 Value of Hong Kong’s re-exports in 2018 Even if US-China trade frictions ease, the near-term outlook for Hong Kong’s merchandise trade remains challenging. Global growth is likely to slow in 2019 (see Chapter 2), which is set to further constrain Hong Kong’s export performance. Various business sentiment indicators show that firms of all sizes are pessimistic about their business outlook (Chart B3.4), with sentiment in the trade sector particularly subdued. Other trade-related sectors, such as logistics, may also be affected. Chart B3.4 Survey of business outlook for Hong Kong’s import and export sector

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades as liquidity tightened amid expectations of seasonal funding demand. Entering 2019, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually weakened, partly because corporates repatriated proceeds raised from initial public offerings and the market rebuilt carry-trade positions, triggering the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March. Nevertheless, Hong Kong dollar trading remained smooth and orderly. Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates generally rose in the second half of 2018, reflecting expectations of US interest rate increases and seasonal funding demand, before falling back in January 2019. Looking ahead, Hong Kong dollar fund flows may become more volatile amid uncertainties including continuing China-US trade tensions, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation. If the Hong Kong dollar-US dollar interest rate differential remains wide, carry-trade activity may persist, causing the Hong Kong dollar to remain weak for some time and possibly triggering the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking again, which would be consistent with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System. After the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate moved away from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until March 2019, when the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered again a total of 4 times (as of March 19) (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate rose briefly in September, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid tighter liquidity, but then gradually declined in October. The Hong Kong dollar stabilised again after November as year-end funding demand tightened liquidity, leading to the unwinding of carry trades. Entering 2019, the spot exchange rate weakened, partly reflecting corporates’ repatriation of proceeds raised from initial public offerings and the market’s rebuilding of carry-trade positions. As the Hong Kong dollar-US dollar interest rate differential widened after the year-end, market participants engaged in carry trades by buying US dollars and selling Hong Kong dollars, causing the Hong Kong dollar to weaken gradually and triggering the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking again in March. Despite the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. The Aggregate Balance had remained at about HK$76.0 billion since August (Chart 4.2), before declining slightly to HK$70.9 billion following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March (as of March 19). Hong Kong dollar fund outflows since April 2018 accounted for only a small portion of the approximately HK$1 trillion of inflows since 2008. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Fund flow indicators The Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index broadly tracked movements in the US dollar and continued to rise during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was very small and therefore had only a limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index, movements in the real effective exchange rate index broadly tracked those in the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates The latest balance of payments statistics showed that portfolio investment continued to record outflows in the third quarter of 2018. Amid weak market sentiment and increased stock market volatility, equity portfolio investment outflows by local residents accelerated, more than offsetting portfolio investment inflows by non-local residents in the third quarter (Table 4.A). By contrast, debt securities investment by both local and non-local residents recorded inflows in the third quarter. Looking ahead, fund flow volatility may intensify amid uncertainties including continuing China-US trade tensions, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation. In addition, the significant negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar may stimulate carry-trade activity and lead to fund outflows. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may weaken and the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking may be triggered again. Fund outflows and the possible triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking are both part of the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System. Despite the continued US interest rate normalisation process and the repeated triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking from April to August, Hong Kong’s monetary conditions remained accommodative in the second half of 2018. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base contracted slightly by 0.7% in the second half, standing at HK$1,632.9 billion at end-2018 (Chart 4.4). The contraction in the Monetary Base was mainly due to the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in August 2018, which reduced the Aggregate Balance from HK$109.5 billion at end-June 2018 to HK$76.4 billion at end-2018, while Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased slightly. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained broadly stable in the first two months of 2019, with no significant change in the Aggregate Balance since August. Subsequently, following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to about HK$70.9 billion (as of March 19). Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base As for broader measures of the Hong Kong dollar money supply, money supply growth generally slowed in the second half, partly reflecting increased uncertainty in the macroeconomic and financial environment. Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (HK$M3) grew by 3.6% in the first half, but increased only slightly by 0.1% in the second half (Chart 4.5). As the main component of HK$M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits were little changed compared with end-June (Chart 4.6).
