Among Hong Kong dollar deposits, demand and savings deposits declined, partly because of fewer investment-related transactions in the second half; on the other hand, time deposits continued to record strong growth owing to higher deposit interest rates. An analysis of counterpart assets showed that the slowdown in HK$M3 growth was due to changes in banks’ capital and reserves (included under “net other items”). Chart 4.5 Changes in HK$M3 and its counterpart assets Foreign currency deposit growth accelerated in the second half. US dollar deposits grew strongly by 8.8% in the second half as banks attracted more deposits after raising preferential US dollar deposit rates, thereby becoming the main driver of foreign currency deposit growth (Chart 4.6). Other foreign currency deposits increased slightly by 1.4% in the second half, with renminbi deposits continuing to grow. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions grew moderately by 3.3% in the second half, slightly faster than the 1.6% increase in the first half. Chart 4.6 Deposit growth Although the Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base and the deposit base remained large, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates began to face some upward pressure in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting US interest rate increases. Seasonal liquidity demand occasionally pushed up short-term interbank rates, making them more volatile than longer-term interbank rates (Chart 4.7). The 3-month and 12-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates averaged 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December, about 30 basis points higher than their June averages. Entering 2019, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates declined overall as seasonal demand subsided. The averages of the 3-month and 12-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates fell to 1.65% and 2.39% respectively in February. Chart 4.7 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted downwards in the second half of 2018, broadly tracking movements in the US dollar yield curve. Compared with end-June 2018, yields on 3-year and 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell by 45 and 37 basis points respectively to 1.56% and 1.83% at end-February 2019 (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Government bond yields, composite interest rate and average interest rate for new mortgages During the review period, the composite interest rate, which measures retail banks’ average cost of Hong Kong dollar funding, rose slightly. Reflecting changes in the cost of interbank and deposit funding, the composite interest rate increased from 0.62% at end-June to 0.89% at end-December 2018, before falling back to 0.83% at end-January 2019 (Chart 4.8). In view of higher funding costs, retail banks raised their best lending rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points after the US federal funds target range was increased in September. However, retail banks did not adjust their best lending rates again after the US federal funds target range was raised once more in December. Meanwhile, the average interest rate for new mortgages rose in tandem with best lending rates to about 2.45% at end-January 2019. Looking ahead, movements in US dollar interest rates, fund flows, and local financial market activities (such as initial public offering subscription activities) will continue to be the main drivers of Hong Kong dollar interest rates. Given that the Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remains large and the banking system holds a substantial amount of Exchange Fund Bills, the pace of increase in Hong Kong dollar interest rates should be relatively moderate, as banks can use Exchange Fund Bills as collateral to borrow Hong Kong dollar funds through the Discount Window. Against the backdrop of escalating China-US trade tensions, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates depreciated against the US dollar from the beginning of 2018 (Chart 4.9). However, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilised in November amid optimism driven by the resumption of high-level trade negotiations between China and the US. Meanwhile, the spread between the onshore and offshore renminbi was not significant during the review period. Chart 4.9 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates At present, continuing China-US trade tensions have not had a material impact on funding conditions in the offshore interbank market. As liquidity conditions remained broadly stable, the overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate stayed below 4% for most of the review period, rising only occasionally owing to seasonal factors (Chart 4.10). The 3-month offshore renminbi interbank rate hovered around 4% between September and December 2018, before falling to 3.02% at end-February 2019, possibly reflecting the monetary easing measures recently introduced by the People’s Bank of China. Nevertheless, the impact of developments in China-US trade negotiations on liquidity in the offshore renminbi interbank market in 2019 remains to be seen. Chart 4.10 Overnight and 3-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate fixings Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half of 2018. The outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew by 3.7% in the second half to RMB657.7 billion at end-2018, slightly faster than the 2.6% increase in the first half (Chart 4.11 and Table 4.B). This was mainly driven by renminbi customer deposits, which grew by 4.5% in the first half and 5.2% in the second half. Among them, corporate customer deposits grew faster than personal customer deposits. However, the outstanding amount of certificates of deposit declined by a further 14.1% in the second half, mainly because fewer certificates of deposit were issued and a relatively large amount matured in October.

Mainly benefiting from an increase in net interest income, retail banks’ profitability continued to improve in the second half of 2018 compared with the same period in 2017. Capital and liquidity positions also remained sound. Reflecting upward pressure on the Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rate and retail deposit rates amid US interest rate normalisation, retail banks’ overall Hong Kong dollar funding costs increased notably, but remained at relatively low levels. Amid an uncertain external environment, bank credit contracted moderately in the second half of 2018. Nevertheless, credit growth showed signs of stabilisation from November onwards, and asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will face multiple headwinds arising from persistent uncertainty over China-US trade relations, slowing global economic growth, uncertainty over the pace of the US monetary policy tightening cycle, and geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should remain vigilant to the impact of a possible further deterioration in the external environment on the credit risk of their related corporate loans. Retail banks’ aggregate pre-tax operating profit increased by 14.3% compared with the same period in 2017, while return on assets rose from 1.14% to 1.23% (Chart 5.1). This strong performance was mainly attributable to a substantial increase in net interest income, which was sufficient to offset increases in loan impairment charges and operating expenses. For 2018 as a whole, retail banks’ aggregate pre-tax operating profit increased by 19.4%, while return on assets rose from 1.16% in 2017 to 1.27%. Chart 5.1 Retail banks’ profitability Retail banks’ net interest margin widened further to 1.67% in the fourth quarter, compared with 1.5% in the same period a year earlier (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Retail banks’ net interest margin Broadly reflecting further US interest rate increases and a decline in interbank Hong Kong dollar liquidity following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in August 2018, Hong Kong interbank funding costs continued to face upward pressure in the second half of 2018. Specifically, the 3-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate rose by 23 basis points in the second half of 2018 (Chart 5.3). As banks generally raised time deposit rates to attract stable, longer-term funding, Hong Kong dollar retail deposit rates also increased during the review period. In addition, following the US interest rate increase decision at the end of September, banks raised their best lending rates and correspondingly increased their savings deposit rates. Given the increases in both wholesale and retail funding costs, the composite interest rate, a measure of retail banks’ average Hong Kong dollar funding cost, rose from 0.62% in June 2018 to 0.89% in December, but remained at a relatively low level by historical standards. Chart 5.3 Interest rates (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Period averages for newly approved loans. More broadly, the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong continued to trend upwards. In the second half of 2018, banks’ average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs increased by 36 basis points, compared with an increase of 40 basis points in the first half (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturity of licensed banks The cumulative rise in the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate exceeded the increase in Hong Kong banks’ overall funding costs, which may have a positive impact on retail banks’ mortgage loans benchmarked against the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate, a type of loan that the industry has actively promoted in recent years. However, further improvement in net interest margins may become more limited, as most mortgage loans benchmarked against the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate have already reached their cap rates benchmarked against the best lending rate. As the timing of future increases in the best lending rate remains uncertain, the continued upward trend in banks’ funding costs amid US interest rate normalisation may weigh on overall net interest margins. Looking ahead, heightened uncertainty in the external environment may cloud banks’ profitability outlook. In particular, against the backdrop of slowing global economic growth, persistent uncertainty over China-US trade relations may dampen business confidence and reduce demand for bank credit. If this results in a significant decline in lending and deterioration in asset quality, it may weigh on banks’ profitability. The Hong Kong banking sector remained well capitalised, far above international minimum standards. At the end of 2018, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorised institutions rose further to 20.3% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 17.9%, of which 16.0% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated authorised institutions 1. Consolidated position. 2. With effect from 1 January 2013, locally incorporated authorised institutions are required to comply with the revised capital framework under Basel III. Accordingly, capital ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with data up to December 2012. In addition to the risk-based capital adequacy ratio, Basel III also introduced a non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement to constrain excessive leverage in the banking system. The minimum leverage ratio requirement came into effect in Hong Kong in 2018, and the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorised institutions remained at a sound level of 8.0% at the end of December 2018, above the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorised institutions As measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement under Basel III, the banking sector’s liquidity position remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions increased from 156.6% in the second quarter of 2018 to 167.6% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 90% applicable in 2018. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions also increased from 51.3% in the second quarter to 54.3% in the fourth quarter, likewise well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio 1. Consolidated position. 2. Quarterly average figures. The Net Stable Funding Ratio, one of the Basel III liquidity standards, indicated stable funding positions among authorised institutions. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 135.6% in the fourth quarter of 2018 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.3%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 50% applicable in 2018. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of authorised institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding a range of liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the main source of funding for authorised institutions, reflecting the stable funding structure maintained by the banking system. At the end of 2018, customer deposits as a share of the total liabilities of all authorised institutions edged up from 54.5% six months earlier to 55.7% (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all authorised institutions 1. Figures may not add up to the total due to rounding. 2. Figures refer to percentages of total liabilities, including capital and reserves. 3. Debt securities include negotiable certificates of deposit and all other negotiable debt instruments. As total loans and advances declined during the second half of 2018 while total deposits increased over the same period, the all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorised institutions fell from 75.7% at the end of June 2018 to 72.6% at year-end (Chart 5.10). Similarly, the foreign-currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorised institutions fell from 65.2% to 58.3% over the same period. In contrast, as growth in Hong Kong dollar deposits was much slower than that in Hong Kong dollar loans, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio edged up from 85.4% at the end of June 2018 to 86.9% at year-end. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of all authorised institutions The interest rate risk exposures of locally incorporated licensed banks declined slightly in the second half of 2018. It is estimated that, under an assumed shock of a general 200-basis-point increase in interest rates, the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions could decline by an amount equivalent to 2.44% of their total capital base at the end of 2018 (Chart 5.11). Nevertheless, given the uncertainty over the pace of further US interest rate increases, banks should closely monitor their interest rate risk management. The interest rate shock refers to the impact of a standard parallel 200-basis-point interest rate shock on institutions’ interest rate risk exposures. 2. The impact of the interest rate shock refers to the impact on the economic value of the banking book and trading book, expressed as a percentage of banks’ total capital base. Against the backdrop of persistent uncertainty over China-US trade tensions, tightening global financial liquidity and slowing global economic growth, credit growth slowed significantly in the second half of 2018. However, credit growth showed signs of stabilisation from November 2018 onwards. On a half-year basis, total loans and advances of all authorised institutions declined by 0.9% in the second half of 2018 after increasing by 5.3% in the first half (Chart 5.12). The decline was attributable to slower growth in domestic lending, including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade finance, and a decrease in loans for use outside Hong Kong. Growth in domestic lending slowed to 0.1% in the second half, while loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.0% over the same period, compared with growth of 5.3% and 5.2% respectively in the preceding six months. For 2018 as a whole, total loan growth slowed markedly from 16.1% in 2017 to 4.4%. Chart 5.12 Loan growth Looking ahead, credit demand may remain weak in the near term. The HKMA’s December 2018 “Survey on Credit Condition Outlook” showed that, among all surveyed authorised institutions, 82% expected loan demand to remain unchanged over the next three months, while the proportion expecting demand to decline rose to 18% (Table 5.A). Despite the slight decline in total loans in the second half of 2018, the asset quality of banks’ loan portfolios remained sound. The gross classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio of all authorised institutions edged down to 0.55% and 0.36% respectively at the end of December 2018, compared with 0.61% and 0.40% respectively at the end of June 2018. For retail banks, the gross classified loan ratio declined slightly to 0.50%, while the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio edged up to 0.32% (Chart 5.13). Both ratios were low by historical standards. Chart 5.13 Asset quality of retail banks 1. Classified loans refer to loans classified as “substandard”, “doubtful” or “loss”. 2. Figures before December 2015 reflect the positions of retail banks’ Hong Kong offices and overseas branches. From December 2015 onwards, the coverage of the figures was expanded to include retail banks’ major overseas subsidiaries. On a half-year basis, growth in personal loans slowed from 5.3% in the first half of 2018 to 3.9% in the second half. This was mainly attributable to slower growth in personal loans, including credit card advances and loans for other private purposes, which offset rapid growth in residential mortgage loans (Table 5.B). As Hong Kong’s nominal gross domestic product grew more slowly than personal loans, the ratio of household debt to gross domestic product edged up from 71.2% in the second quarter of 2018 to 71.9% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.14).

The coronavirus outbreak that began in early 2020 has hit both demand and supply, posing challenges to the global economy that differ from those of previous crises. Although major central banks and some governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March to contain the economic shock caused by the outbreak, financial markets have remained volatile and global financial conditions have tightened. Despite uncertainties in the external and domestic environments, Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and orderly. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remaining strong, the Aggregate Balance stable and total deposits growing moderately, no noticeable fund outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or Hong Kong's banking system were observed during the review period. After a moderate rebound in the first half of 2019, growth in total loans slowed in the second half. The residential property market generally softened from mid-2019, although its movements were somewhat volatile. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future China-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions and local social incidents. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and household debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, global economic growth had shown initial signs of stabilisation, benefiting from greater monetary easing by major central banks, an easing of China-US trade tensions and a reduced risk of a “no-deal Brexit” in the United Kingdom. However, the continuing increase in coronavirus infections worldwide since late January has raised market concerns and triggered sharp volatility in global financial markets. In response to the evolving risks from the outbreak, several major central banks substantially cut interest rates and expanded liquidity facilities, while some governments also introduced targeted measures to support the real economy. Nevertheless, global financial conditions tightened amid widening credit spreads and sharp falls in equity markets. Looking ahead, downside risks to the global economic outlook have increased. The coronavirus outbreak will weigh on global economic activity, and the extent of the economic shock will depend on the severity and duration of the outbreak. Over the medium term, tensions between the United States and its major trading partners may re-emerge, while the United Kingdom may also face difficult trade negotiations with the European Union after Brexit. Weak global demand continued to weigh on economic growth in East Asia1. East Asia's exports to major destinations including the United States, European economies and Mainland China remained weak in the second half of 2019. Some major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region recently reported revenue growth, but whether there will be a broad-based recovery in the technology product cycle remains to be seen. Financial markets reacted positively to the phase one China-US trade agreement announced in December 2019, with the trade truce reducing global trade uncertainty to some extent. Nevertheless, East Asia will continue to face headwinds including weak corporate earnings and high private-sector leverage ratios. Meanwhile, the coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that regional economies may come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. Travel bans imposed by several economies in the region may weigh on Asia's tourism industry, particularly in economies that rely more heavily on exports of tourism services. Given the region's close supply-chain links with Mainland China, the manufacturing sector may also be affected by the outbreak. As for Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 owing to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the phase one China-US trade agreement will help temporarily reduce external uncertainties facing the Mainland economy, downside pressures remain amid the coronavirus outbreak, continued economic rebalancing and the global economic slowdown. The Central Economic Work Conference convened in December 2019 made economic stability a priority for 2020, while also emphasising the containment of financial risks. The latest consensus forecasts indicate that Mainland economic growth will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, Mainland authorities continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policies to support the private sector, particularly small private enterprises. Despite these measures, some media reports and market analysts noted that private industrial enterprises may have experienced a decline in shareholders' equity in recent years, which was regarded as a sign of a “private-sector retreat”. Box 2 examines the drivers of changes in the equity of Mainland industrial enterprises using 2018 listed-company data and finds that private or small enterprises are not inherently more susceptible to downsizing or “retreat”. Although the study finds that negative earnings are the largest driver, other factors, particularly structural factors, also warrant attention (see Box 2 for details). Hong Kong's economic activity contracted markedly in the second half of 2019. Real Gross Domestic Product declined for three consecutive quarters, indicating that the Hong Kong economy had entered a recession. As a result, the economy contracted by 1.2% for 2019 as a whole, compared with growth of 2.9% in 2018, marking the first annual contraction since 2009. Slower domestic demand, particularly a contraction in private consumption, was the main drag on Gross Domestic Product in the second half of 2019. Local social incidents severely affected consumption activity, resulting in a weak economic outlook that in turn undermined consumer and business confidence. With a renewed escalation in China-US trade frictions, slower global economic growth and a severe downturn in inbound tourism, Hong Kong's external trade performance remained subdued. In view of the strong economic headwinds, the Government introduced multiple rounds of economic stimulus measures between August and December 2019. To give banks more room to step up support for the domestic economy and help smooth the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October that the Countercyclical Capital Buffer ratio for banks would be lowered from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion of lending capacity to enterprises, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, while the recent outbreak has also introduced substantial downside risks. As sectors including retail, accommodation services, food services, tourism and transport have yet to recover from the disruption caused by the social incidents, the outbreak will deal a double blow to these sectors. However, the package of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget could provide relief to households and businesses, particularly SMEs, including a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and concessionary low-interest loans to enterprises under the “SME Financing Guarantee Scheme” with a 100% Government guarantee.2 On 16 March 2020, the HKMA further lowered the Countercyclical Capital Buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0%, giving banks more room to step up support for the domestic economy, particularly sectors and individuals facing greater short-term pressure owing to the outbreak. Analysed by components of Gross Domestic Product, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak because of fragile consumer and business confidence. Although government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to remain relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the phase one China-US trade agreement is expected to have a mildly positive effect on the domestic economy in the short term.3 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may disrupt regional supply chains and slow cross-border economic activity, such as tourism, thereby constraining Hong Kong's export performance. The Government forecasts real Gross Domestic Product growth of between -1.5% and 0.5% in 2020, while the average growth forecast of international organisations and private-sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including slower global economic growth, China-US trade relations, Mainland China's economic performance and local social incidents. The labour market came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020, with total employment declining, the unemployment rate rising and the real wage index falling year on year. Specifically, the unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partly reflecting the impact of the social incidents and the outbreak on the retail, accommodation and food services sectors. Looking ahead, the unemployment rate will rise further given the weak economic outlook and the coronavirus outbreak. Box 3 discusses recent labour-market developments and the short-term outlook in greater detail. Domestic inflationary pressures continued to build through the third quarter of 2019, mainly owing to increases in fresh pork prices; inflation momentum then gradually moderated as economic activity weakened. Inflation is expected to ease in the near term amid weak economic conditions, consolidation in private residential rents and moderate imported inflation. Consensus forecasts for headline inflation in 2020 range from 0.6% to 3.7%, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation at 2.5%. Supported by increased equity-related demand for the Hong Kong dollar, including initial public offerings, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually strengthened from mid-October 2019. Entering December, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gained further upward momentum, partly because of buoyant initial public offering activity and partly because tighter liquidity towards year-end prompted the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened slightly towards the end of February. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly during the review period, without triggering the Convertibility Undertaking. The Aggregate Balance remained stable at about HK$54 billion. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates have fluctuated, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital-market activity such as initial public offerings. Box 4 examines how market attention to forthcoming initial public offering activity affects the 3-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate. Meanwhile, the composite interest rate gradually rose from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020, reflecting banks' continued increases in preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funding. As some banks raised the interest-rate caps benchmarked to the best lending rate, the average interest rate on new mortgages rose to around 2.6% in October, but fell slightly to around 2.5% by January 2020 as best lending rates in the market were lowered from November onwards. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remaining strong, the Aggregate Balance stable and total deposits growing moderately, no noticeable fund outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or Hong Kong's banking system were observed during the review period. Nevertheless, the impact of any further deterioration in the coronavirus outbreak amid uncertainties in the external environment needs to be monitored. With ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, the HKMA has the capability, resources and determination to cope with capital outflows and maintain monetary and financial stability in Hong Kong. During the review period, expectations of a China-US trade agreement strengthened both the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates, but they came under depreciation pressure from late January 2020 owing to the coronavirus outbreak. In the latter part of 2019, the offshore renminbi generally traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi. The discount briefly widened at the end of January 2020, but the spread remained moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool recovered slightly after a mild decline in the previous review period. At the end of January 2020, renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased to RMB637.4 billion. Hong Kong's other renminbi businesses also expanded, with strong growth in local renminbi bank lending and renminbi trade settlement business. The average daily turnover of the Renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high at RMB1,133.9 billion for 2019 as a whole. Despite uncertainties in the external environment, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continued opening of the Mainland's capital account, increased allocation to renminbi assets by international investors, and deeper regional economic and financial cooperation under the “Belt and Road” and “Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area” initiatives.

At the end of 2019, global economic activity showed signs of stabilising, raising market expectations of a global economic recovery. However, the continued increase in global coronavirus infections since late January 2020 dashed hopes of a recovery and deepened investors’ concerns about a global recession, triggering a sell-off in global financial markets. In response to the economic shock, major central banks and some governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March. In view of the spread of the pandemic, downside risks to the global economic growth outlook have increased. In East Asia, weak global demand since the second half of 2019 clouded the outlook for the region’s economies. The coronavirus outbreak is expected to weigh on regional economic growth in the short term, with the tourism industry particularly hard hit. Meanwhile, East Asia continues to face the challenges of weak corporate earnings and elevated private-sector leverage ratios. In Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 amid weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the phase one trade agreement between China and the US will help temporarily reduce external uncertainties, downward pressure remains in the face of the coronavirus outbreak, continued economic rebalancing and the global economic slowdown, while the authorities’ monetary and fiscal policy responses will provide some cushion. Amid persistent trade tensions and policy uncertainty, manufacturing and investment remained weak, and global economic growth was still lacklustre in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, economic growth showed preliminary signs of stabilising in the final quarter (Chart 2.1), partly benefiting from the earlier monetary easing by the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, as well as the easing of global trade tensions following the signing of the China-US “phase one” trade agreement. Chart 2.1 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index However, since the end of January, the continued rise in coronavirus infections worldwide and the ensuing economic shock have caused market concerns and triggered a sell-off in global financial markets (Chart 2.2). Given that Mainland China is a major global export destination and occupies an important position in global supply chains, disruptions to its production activities and the resulting drag on its economic growth will generate significant spillovers that could spread worldwide (Chart 2.3). Since late February, coronavirus infections have surged outside Mainland China, which could exacerbate supply-chain disruptions and create the risk of a direct drag on local economic activity.5 Chart 2.2 MSCI All Country World Index and Bloomberg Barclays Global Corporate Bond Index option-adjusted spread Chart 2.3 Exports of goods and services to Mainland China by selected major advanced economies in 2018 (as a percentage of their gross domestic product) In response to the potentially severe economic impact of the pandemic, some central banks, including the US Federal Reserve, the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England, have cut interest rates since early March, while some governments have also introduced targeted measures to support households and businesses. However, financial markets remain under tremendous selling pressure, leading to a marked tightening in global financial conditions, which may in turn exacerbate downward pressure on the global economy (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Bloomberg Advanced Economies Financial Conditions Index In addition to developments in the pandemic, other downside risks and uncertainties also cloud the global economic outlook. In particular, regarding trade tensions, although policy risks have declined following the phase one trade agreement between China and the US, subsequent negotiations may be fraught with difficulties as many thorny structural issues remain unresolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the European Union and the United Kingdom are not expected to proceed smoothly, thereby prolonging post-Brexit uncertainty. In addition, the sharp decline in oil prices since March will put pressure on major oil-exporting emerging market economies. In East Asia, real economic activity remained weak in the second half of 2019 owing to subdued global demand. The region’s exports to major destinations, including the US, European economies and Mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Chart 2.5). Although preliminary signs suggested that the downturn in the region’s technology-product cycle was bottoming out, including reports by some large regional electronics companies of improved earnings at the end of 2019,6 it remained to be seen whether exports of technology products in the region had staged a substantive rebound. Chart 2.5 East Asia: merchandise exports to major destinations Persistent weakness in economic growth and trade uncertainty also weighed on investor sentiment, with gross fixed capital formation declining in most East Asian economies in 2019 (Chart 2.6), potentially affecting the region’s potential economic growth over the longer term. To support economic growth amid moderate inflation, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines and Korea lowered their policy rates again in the second half of 2019 after cutting rates in the first half, while the Bank of Thailand also lowered its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Chart 2.6 East Asia: gross fixed capital formation The coronavirus outbreak raised concerns that the region’s economies could come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. As several economies in the region imposed travel restrictions on Mainland China, the tourism industry bore the brunt, particularly economies more dependent on visitors from Mainland China and exports of travel services, which were more severely affected by the outbreak (Chart 2.7). A prolonged and worsening outbreak would also affect regional supply chains closely linked to Mainland China. Chart 2.7 East Asia: tourism exports and Chinese tourists In the short term, the outbreak will continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment. Based on the experience of the 2003 SARS outbreak, these effects may be temporary, but the actual outcome will depend on the severity and geographical spread of the outbreak, as well as the effectiveness of government actions to contain it. Meanwhile, East Asian economies also face multiple headwinds. First, although corporate earnings are expected by the market to deteriorate in the short term (Chart 2.8), accommodative global monetary conditions have encouraged the search for yield, thereby pushing up asset prices without support from fundamentals. As a result, regional equity markets are more vulnerable to shifts in investor sentiment. Chart 2.8 Expected earnings of constituents of benchmark equity indices Second, weak corporate earnings and economic growth may make it more difficult for the region’s private sector to service its debt. Although lower domestic interest rates can provide breathing room for indebted companies and households, they may also sow the seeds for further debt accumulation. In addition, as discussed in Box 1, the risk of debt accumulation in the private sector may also intensify as more index-tracking funds flow into the region’s financial markets, although this impact may be limited to firms with sounder financial fundamentals and their long-term borrowing. Third, in terms of external factors, the risks facing East Asian economies may also increase amid an increasingly protectionist US trade policy. Despite recent progress on the phase one trade agreement between China and the US, China-US trade tensions persist as the fundamental trade issues between the two countries remain unresolved. The widening trade surpluses of several regional economies with the US (Chart 2.9) suggest that multinational corporations may continue to seek more sources of supply outside China-centred supply chains to circumvent tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus of nine emerging Asian economies (excluding China) with the US had risen to approximately US$167 billion. If their trade surpluses with the US continue to widen, the relevant Asian economies could become the next targets of the trade war; for example, the US Government imposed hefty tariffs of up to 456% on Vietnamese steel imports in July 2019.7 In view of this, despite the China-US trade truce, the regional trade outlook remains highly uncertain. Chart 2.9 Merchandise trade surplus with the US Over the past decade, greater integration of international financial markets has led to a significant increase in global cross-border portfolio investment flows. A recent study found that up to 70% of these cross-border investment flows were driven by index-driven funds.8 Index-driven funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices (commonly known as passive funds), but also actively managed funds that use investment indices as references.9 By bringing in overseas investors whom the relevant economies could not otherwise attract or reach, these funds help promote the development of financial markets in emerging market economies. As a result, such funds enable emerging market economies to diversify their investor bases, contributing to long-term market growth and stability. But is there really such a thing as a free lunch? Regarding passive bond funds, there are concerns that investments by such funds may weaken the financial discipline of the corporate bond issuers in which they invest, thereby leading to high leverage among the relevant firms.10 In addition, it has been argued that the growth of index-driven funds in recent years has exacerbated volatility in global portfolio investment flows, making emerging market economies, which are already highly sensitive to global factors and affected by other common factors, more vulnerable.11 This box evaluates the financial stability implications of index-driven investment in relation to these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investment funds to the relevant bonds according to the weights of constituent bonds in the benchmark index. Therefore, compared with actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions adopted by passive bond funds may leave issuers of index-constituent bonds with little incentive to act in the interests of fund investors.13 Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, such behaviour may encourage excessive borrowing, posing significant credit and debt-servicing risks to the corporate sectors of emerging market economies, where leverage ratios have risen sharply since the global financial crisis (Chart B1.1). Chart B1.1 Corporate leverage in emerging market economies Using the weights of firms in individual emerging market economies in a major index tracking emerging market corporate bonds as an estimate of the extent to which their bonds are invested in by passive bond funds,14 we find that an increase in such investment raises the long-term, rather than short-term, leverage ratios of the corporate issuers of the relevant bonds. The solid blue bars in Chart B1.2 show the estimated effects. Apart from promoting the development of corporate bond markets in emerging market economies, the expanded long-term bond investor base resulting from passive bond funds is also conducive to the development of firms in emerging market economies. We also find that the above effects are significant only for firms in emerging market economies with sounder fundamentals, particularly stronger debt-servicing capacity and lower leverage ratios (the solid green bars in Chart B1.2). Faced with higher costs of financial distress, highly leveraged firms or those with weaker debt-servicing capacity appear less likely to fall further into a debt trap as a result of investment by passive bond funds. Overall, the above findings suggest that growth in passive bond fund investment may not substantially increase debt-servicing risks in the corporate sectors of emerging market economies.

Owing to weaker private consumption, reduced investment spending and poor export performance, the Hong Kong economy contracted in the second half of 2019 and entered its first recession since 2009. The economy is expected to face significant challenges in 2020, while the recent coronavirus outbreak has also brought notable downside risks. The economic outlook is being affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including slower global economic growth, China-US trade relations, the economic performance of Mainland China and developments in local social incidents. Given the various headwinds facing the economy, the unemployment rate is likely to rise further in 2020. Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease, although the outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. The Hong Kong economy contracted markedly in the second half of 2019. On a year-on-year basis, real Gross Domestic Product contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters respectively (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the economic contraction in the second half, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the year as a whole, compared with growth of 2.9% in 2018, marking the first annual contraction since the 2009 global financial crisis. Chart 3.1 Real Gross Domestic Product growth and contributions from major expenditure components On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity slowed markedly in the second half (Chart 3.1). Specifically, real Gross Domestic Product declined successively by 0.4%, 3.0% and 0.3% in the second, third and fourth quarters, indicating that the economy had entered a recession. On the domestic front, private consumption was the main drag on Gross Domestic Product in the third quarter. Local social incidents severely affected consumption activity, while the resultant weakening of the economic outlook dampened consumer confidence, causing private consumption to contract markedly from the third quarter onwards. 33 Amid increased economic uncertainties and deteriorating business sentiment, total investment spending remained weak and dragged down Gross Domestic Product in the fourth quarter. 34 On the external front, Hong Kong’s external trade performance remained subdued amid escalating China-US trade tensions, weakening global economic growth and a sharp decline in visitor arrivals (Chart 3.2). 35 Affected by the sharp contraction in exports of services, net exports dragged down Gross Domestic Product in the third quarter, but supported Gross Domestic Product growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the goods trade balance. Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports Given the substantial headwinds facing the economy, the Government introduced several rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to ease the financial burden on the public, safeguard employment and support enterprises, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and severely affected sectors such as retail, food services, transport and tourism. 36 To give banks greater room to step up support for the local economy and help mitigate the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October that the Countercyclical Capital Buffer ratio for banks would be reduced from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion in lending capacity to enterprises, including SMEs. Hong Kong’s economy is expected to face significant challenges in 2020, while the recent outbreak has also brought notable downside risks. As some sectors have yet to recover from the disruption caused by the social incidents, the outbreak will deal a double blow to these sectors. Nevertheless, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide assistance to households and enterprises, particularly SMEs, including a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and concessionary low-interest loans to enterprises with a 100% Government guarantee under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. 37 The HKMA’s further reduction of the Countercyclical Capital Buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0% on 16 March 2020 will give banks greater room to step up support for the local economy, particularly sectors and individuals facing greater short-term pressure as a result of the outbreak. Analysed by components of Gross Domestic Product, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak because of fragile consumer and business confidence. Although government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. Regarding external factors, the China-US phase one trade agreement is expected to have a modest positive impact on the local economy in the short term. 38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong’s external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may cause disruptions to regional supply chains and a slowdown in cross-border economic activities, such as tourism, thereby constraining Hong Kong’s export performance. The Government forecasts real Gross Domestic Product growth of between -1.5% and 0.5% in 2020, while the growth forecasts of international organisations and private-sector analysts average -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to the numerous uncertainties and risks described in the preceding chapters. The labour market came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and climbed further to 3.7% in February 2020 (Chart 3.3). In particular, the unemployment rate in the retail, accommodation and food services sectors rose to a nearly ten-year high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe impact of the social incidents. 39 As economic momentum weakened, total employment declined by 0.5% year on year in the second half of 2019 and continued to fall to 3,768,800 in February 2020. The decline in employment was mainly attributable to the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food services and construction sectors. Real wages also fell by 0.3% year on year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, in view of the weak economic outlook described above, the labour market will continue to face greater challenges, and the unemployment rate is very likely to rise further. Box 3 examines in greater detail the recent developments and near-term outlook of the labour market. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Local inflationary pressures continued to build up until the third quarter of 2019, mainly owing to the impact of rising fresh pork prices; thereafter, as economic activity weakened, inflation momentum also gradually slowed. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index rose by 3.3% in the third quarter, with the increase easing slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also eased from a peak of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The slowdown in inflation momentum was due to reduced price pressures across a number of Consumer Price Index components. For tradable goods, underlying food inflation remained notable because of rising fresh pork prices, but price pressures on consumer goods such as clothing and footwear and durable goods remained moderate. For services, as growth in newly contracted private residential rents slowed earlier, growth in the rental component of the Consumer Price Index also trended downwards (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures increased slightly but remained moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different indicators of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index and market rents Chart 3.6 Unit labour costs Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease in the near term. On the domestic front, weak economic conditions and a widening negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on local inflation. As private residential rental growth continues to slow, the housing rental component of inflation should ease further. On the external front, imported inflation is expected to remain moderate owing to weak global economic growth and soft energy prices. Market consensus forecasts headline inflation in 2020 to range between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation at 2.5% and headline inflation at 1.7%. This inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. On the one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, a more severe-than-expected economic deterioration, for example due to the persistence of the coronavirus outbreak, may further suppress inflation. On the other hand, more severe disruptions to the supply of fresh pork would exert upward pressure on inflation. Despite the marked slowdown in the Hong Kong economy, the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8-2.9% in the first nine months of 2019. It was only as the social incidents persisted that the unemployment rate rose more noticeably to 3.3% by the end of 2019. Affected by the coronavirus outbreak, the labour market will face greater headwinds in 2020. Against this backdrop, this Box analyses recent labour market developments and the near-term outlook, including why the overall labour market remained broadly resilient in the first three quarters of 2019, with the unemployment rate virtually unchanged, and the implications for future developments. It also examines some risk factors that could cause the unemployment rate to rise sharply. It is worth noting that the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator, partly because adjusting labour demand entails costs. In fact, the unemployment rate tends to lag the year-on-year growth rate of real Gross Domestic Product by about two to three quarters (Chart B3.1). This lagging nature may explain why the unemployment rate remained low at around 2.9% when real economic activity deteriorated sharply in the third quarter. Chart B3.1 Real Gross Domestic Product growth and the unemployment rate On the labour demand side, although China-US trade tensions and local social incidents dealt a severe blow to employment in the trade sector and the retail- and tourism-related sectors respectively, some major sectors continued to support the overall labour market. Specifically, employment in the financial, business, public administration, social and personal services sectors continued to grow in 2019, partly offsetting the impact of declines in employment in the trade and retail sectors (Chart B3.2). Despite the economy entering a recession, Hong Kong’s financial system remained robust, while financial activities relating to fintech development and initial public offerings were also highly active. These factors may have helped support the employment market in the financial and business services sectors. In addition, public administration, social and personal services, including education, healthcare and social work activities, appear to be less sensitive to the economic cycle. Correlation analysis shows that while employment in many sectors is highly correlated with real Gross Domestic Product, public administration, social and personal services respond more neutrally to the economic cycle. In other words, employment in these sectors may not be greatly affected by cyclical factors even when the economy slows. Chart B3.2 Changes in employment by sector in 2019 On the labour supply side, the labour force participation rate 40 declined from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer against an increase in the unemployment rate. Chart B3.3 shows the various supply and demand factors contributing to changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labour force participation rate (green bar) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019. 41 On the other hand, the increase in employment in the first half of 2019 (purple bar) also helped contain the unemployment rate. However, as the economy contracted markedly in the second half, the decline in employment exerted upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Overall, although employment declined during the recession, the lower labour force participation rate helped alleviate the pressure for the unemployment rate to rise in the second half of 2019. Chart B3.3 Factors contributing to changes in the unemployment rate Some changes in the structure of the labour market also warrant attention. In particular, the increased share of voluntary part-time employees may help companies retain staff. In fact, the shares of self-employed and underemployed persons in total employment declined in recent years to 6% and 1% respectively, while the number of voluntary part-time employees continued to rise, becoming the second-largest group within total employment (around 7% in 2017). 42 Companies may therefore be able to retain or hire more employees by adjusting the working hours of part-time employees. Our calculations show that average weekly working hours have declined from a recent peak of 48 hours in 2010 to around 44 hours at present, partly reflecting the larger number of part-time workers in the current employed population.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has strengthened since October, with the upward momentum increasing further in December, keeping the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone in recent months. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar partly stemmed from equity-related demand and partly from the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions prompted by tighter liquidity towards year-end. Overall, Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and orderly. Although the coronavirus outbreak could trigger market sentiment and lead to greater volatility in fund flows amid an uncertain external environment, Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, and is therefore capable of withstanding fund outflow pressures without compromising local financial stability. Supported by increased equity-related demand for the Hong Kong dollar, including initial public offerings, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has gradually strengthened since mid-October (Chart 4.1). Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar increased further, and from mid-December to February, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone. The strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate was partly attributable to buoyant initial public offering activity and partly to the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions prompted by tighter liquidity towards year-end. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on February 28. Overall, trading in the Hong Kong dollar continued to be smooth and orderly during the review period. As neither the strong-side nor weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered during the review period, the Aggregate Balance remained unchanged at approximately HK$54 billion (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar broadly tracked movements in the US dollar and edged up during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was very small and therefore had a limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar, the real effective exchange rate index broadly tracked the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates When measuring fund flows in Hong Kong, it is necessary to distinguish between two distinct but interrelated concepts of fund flows: (1) Hong Kong dollar fund flows; and (2) cross-border fund flows. Hong Kong dollar fund flows focus on the monetary dimension of fund flows and help assess monetary stability, particularly under the Linked Exchange Rate System. Cross-border fund flows, on the other hand, focus on the geographical movement of funds through Hong Kong’s banking system, which helps assess the stability of Hong Kong’s overall financial system. The two fund flow concepts require different monitoring indicators. When monitoring Hong Kong dollar fund flows, attention should be paid to the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate and the Aggregate Balance. If the public or investors convert a large amount of their Hong Kong dollar assets into foreign currency assets, demand for the Hong Kong dollar will naturally decline, causing the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate to weaken. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, if the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakens to the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking rate of HK$7.85 per US dollar, the HKMA will stand ready to buy Hong Kong dollars at the request of banks, thereby reducing the Aggregate Balance. Since April 2019, the Aggregate Balance has remained broadly unchanged, while the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has been on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone in recent months. Therefore, no significant outflows from the Hong Kong dollar were observed during the review period. When monitoring cross-border fund flows, total deposits in Hong Kong’s banking system are a useful indicator. When substantial funds flow out of Hong Kong’s banking system, bank deposits will inevitably decline. During the review period, total deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating that there were no significant cross-border fund outflows. Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and orderly, indicating that the impact of the coronavirus outbreak on Hong Kong’s monetary conditions remained limited. Nevertheless, the risks arising from the coronavirus outbreak need to be closely monitored. With ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, the HKMA has the capability, resources and resolve to cope with fund outflows and maintain monetary and financial stability in Hong Kong. Despite an uncertain external environment and a slowdown in the local economy, Hong Kong’s monetary conditions remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base remained sizeable, increasing by 4.0% from end-June to HK$1,689.4 billion at end-January 2020 (Chart 4.4). As no Convertibility Undertaking was triggered during this period, the Aggregate Balance remained broadly unchanged at approximately HK$54 billion. Other components of the monetary base, including outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, Certificates of Indebtedness, and government-issued notes and coins in circulation, increased steadily. Chart 4.4 Components of the monetary base During the review period, the broad Hong Kong dollar money supply indicators remained broadly stable. Broad Hong Kong dollar money supply (HK$M3) grew by 3.5% in the first half of 2019, before edging up by 0.2% over the seven-month period since end-June 2019. An analysis of counterpart assets shows that the growth in HK$M3 since end-June mainly reflected an increase in banks’ net foreign currency assets and an expansion in the monetary base, driven by increases in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued notes and coins in circulation (Chart 4.5). Over the seven-month period since end-June, Hong Kong dollar deposits, the main component of HK$M3, remained broadly unchanged (Chart 4.6). Among Hong Kong dollar deposits, time deposits continued to grow moderately, partly reflecting higher Hong Kong dollar deposit rates. Chart 4.5 Changes in HK$M3 and counterpart assets Over the seven-month period since end-June 2019, foreign currency deposits grew moderately by 2.3% (Chart 4.6), mainly driven by US dollar deposits, which increased by 3.5% during the period. Other foreign currency deposits declined by 1.0% over the same period, with renminbi deposits recording a slight decline in Hong Kong dollar terms. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions grew steadily by 1.2% since end-June. Supported by the increase in total deposits, Hong Kong’s total broad money supply also increased at a relatively steady pace, with total money supply M2 and M3 rising by 1.6% and 1.5%, respectively, since end-June (Chart 4.7). As monthly monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various short-term factors, such as seasonal and initial public offering-related funding demand, as well as business- and investment-related activities, the statistics should be interpreted with caution. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions by currency Chart 4.7 Aggregate broad money supply (M2) Although monetary conditions remained relatively accommodative, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates fluctuated, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activity since the fourth quarter of 2019. In particular, as initial public offering activity in Hong Kong’s stock market became more active, the Hong Kong dollar overnight interbank offered rate experienced relatively large fluctuations in late October and mid-November (Chart 4.8).44 During the review period, other short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates generally increased. Subscriptions for large new listings can exert significant pressure on overnight rates. An empirical analysis in Box 4 shows that market attention to future initial public offering activity also affects the 3-month Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rate. This occurs if market participants anticipate future subscription closing dates for large new listings and prepare medium-term funds in advance. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank offered rates As for the Hong Kong dollar yield curve, it shifted downwards in tandem with the US dollar yield curve. Compared with end-June 2019, the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell by 60 basis points to 1.04% on February 28, 2020 (Chart 4.9). Meanwhile, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell by 50 basis points over the same period to 1.00%. Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, composite interest rate and average interest rate on new mortgages At the retail level, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, gradually increased from 0.94% at end-July 2019 to 1.01% at end-January 2020. The increase mainly reflected banks’ continued raising of preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funding, resulting in an increase in the weighted Hong Kong dollar deposit rate. Following the reduction in the target range for the US federal funds rate at end-October 2019, several retail banks lowered their best lending rates by 12.5 basis points. As a result, retail banks’ best lending rates currently range from 5.00% to 5.50%. Regarding mortgage loans benchmarked against the Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rate, major banks raised the interest-rate cap determined by the best lending rate, and the average interest rate on new mortgages therefore increased to around 2.63% in October.45 As the best lending rates in the market were lowered from November onwards, the average mortgage interest rate subsequently declined slightly to 2.53% in January 2020. In response to the evolving risks posed by the coronavirus outbreak to US economic activity and to support the US Federal Reserve in achieving its policy objectives, the Federal Reserve lowered the target range for the federal funds rate by a total of 150 basis points to 0-0.25% on March 3 (US time) and March 15 (US time). Although Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates track movements in US dollar interest rates over the long term, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates may be affected by local factors that could influence demand for the Hong Kong dollar, such as new listing activity in Hong Kong. As the Aggregate Balance of the banking system has declined since April 2018, the sensitivity of Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates to changes in the supply of and demand for Hong Kong dollar funds may have increased. However, this does not mean that the current Aggregate Balance of HK$54 billion is insufficient to meet interbank payment and settlement needs. In fact, Hong Kong’s interbank market has continued to operate in an orderly manner. If short-term liquidity tightens, banks can make use of the liquidity facilities provided by the HKMA. Given the possibility of an escalation in China-US trade tensions, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened significantly in late August and September 2019, with the offshore renminbi falling to a ten-year low of 7.19 against the US dollar on September 2 (Chart 4.10). Entering October, market expectations that China and the US would resume trade negotiations reversed the renminbi’s depreciation trend. The offshore and onshore renminbi strengthened in the fourth quarter and briefly rose past the 6.9 level in mid-January 2020 following the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US. However, since end-January, the offshore and onshore renminbi have again faced weakening pressure due to the coronavirus outbreak. The offshore renminbi traded at a discount to the onshore renminbi for most of the period from May to August, but generally traded at a premium later in 2019. The discount widened briefly at end-January 2020, although the spread between the two remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates Despite fluctuations in the renminbi exchange rate, liquidity conditions in the offshore renminbi interbank market remained broadly stable. During the review period, the 3-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong interbank offered rate continued to hover between 3-4% (Chart 4.11). The overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong interbank offered rate fluctuated briefly in late August and late November due to MSCI’s A-share adjustments, and at end-January 2020 near the Lunar New Year holiday.

Amid increasing uncertainties in the global and domestic economic environment, the profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong recorded a slight decline in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, the capital and liquidity positions of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and sound by international standards. Asset quality remained healthy by historical standards. Although growth in total loans slowed in the second half of last year, it still outpaced deposit growth during the review period. Accordingly, the average loan-to-deposit ratio in all currencies and the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions both increased. However, given the stable level of the Aggregate Balance of the banking system and broadly steady deposits, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face a number of downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future China-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions and local social incidents. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify. In the second half of 2019, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks59 declined slightly by 1.5% compared with the same period in 2018. Accordingly, the return on assets edged down to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, from 1.23% in the same period in 2018 (Chart 5.1). Although the net interest margin of retail banks narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the corresponding period of 2019 (Chart 5.2), their net interest income continued to record moderate growth during the review period. However, increases in loan impairment provisions and operating expenses of retail banks led to a slight decline in profitability. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Despite three cuts of 25 basis points each in the US federal funds target rate in the second half of 2019, the Hong Kong dollar wholesale funding market has yet to experience significant downward pressure. On the contrary, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates have been on an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019, driven by a number of local factors, including seasonal funding demand, increased liquidity demand arising from large initial public offerings, and tighter liquidity conditions in the interbank market. Meanwhile, longer-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates remained broadly stable during the review period, with the three-month HIBOR standing at 2.43% at the end of 2019, close to its level six months earlier (blue line in Chart 5.3). At the retail level, as Hong Kong dollar savings deposit rates remained close to zero, retail banks had limited room to follow US policy rate cuts by lowering their rates.60 On the other hand, as Hong Kong dollar liquidity in the banking system tightened during the review period, banks continued to compete for long-term and stable deposit funding.61 Reflecting the increase in the weighted funding cost of Hong Kong dollar deposits, the composite interest rate, an indicator of the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks, gradually rose from 0.95% six months earlier to 1.09% at the end of 2019, although it remained low by historical standards (green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates From a broader perspective, as the decline in the US dollar funding cost of locally licensed banks offset the slight increase in their Hong Kong dollar funding cost, their average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost edged down by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019 (Chart 5.4). During the review period, banks’ net interest income benefited from the slight decline in their overall funding cost and the relatively high level of Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates, supporting banking-sector profitability over the same period. Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost and maturity of licensed banks 1. Since June 2019, all licensed banks subject to the new local interest rate risk in the banking book framework have submitted returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks have continued to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. The overall funding cost and maturity have been calculated as weighted averages of the relevant figures for these two groups of licensed banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards are not directly comparable with those for earlier months. Looking ahead, a number of downside risk factors in the external and domestic environment will continue to cloud banks’ profitability outlook. These include uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future direction of China-US trade relations and escalating geopolitical tensions. An intensification of these risk factors could undermine already weak global economic growth momentum and reduce demand for bank credit. Given the widespread adoption of accommodative monetary policies by major central banks, the global low-interest-rate environment may persist, potentially putting pressure on banks’ future net interest margins. Domestically, local social incidents since mid-2019 have continued to weigh on business investment and market confidence. Against an already weak economic backdrop, if the situation persists or deteriorates further, the outlook for credit demand and banks’ asset quality could worsen. In terms of overall market developments, following the issuance of eight virtual bank licences by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Hong Kong banking sector began rolling out virtual banking services. As these new market participants may seek to increase their market shares by offering more convenient products and more attractive deposit rates to attract new customers, this could exert upward pressure on the funding costs of incumbent banks. Although the short-term impact may remain moderate because virtual banks currently operate on a limited scale, the longer-term impact may depend on whether incumbent banks accelerate the adoption of financial technology to remain competitive. The results of Box 5 show that the extent of financial technology adoption by Hong Kong banks is statistically associated with improvements in their cost efficiency and profitability. The capitalization of the Hong Kong banking sector remained sound and well above minimum international standards. At the end of 2019, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions rose further to 20.7% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 18.5%, of which 16.5% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalization of locally incorporated authorized institutions In addition to the risk-based capital adequacy ratio, Basel III also imposes a non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement to constrain excessive leverage in the banking system. The leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a sound level of 8.2% at the end of 2019, above the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions As measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio65 requirement, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions rose from 152.8% in the second quarter of 2019 to 159.9% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions also increased moderately from 54.6% in the second quarter of 2019 to around 56.3% in the fourth quarter of 2019, well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The Net Stable Funding Ratio66, one of the Basel III liquidity standards, indicated that the funding positions of authorized institutions were stable. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 131.7% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.5%, also above the statutory minimum requirement of 75% applicable in 2019. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding a wide range of liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the main source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting the stable funding structure of the banking system. At the end of 2019, customer deposits as a proportion of the total liabilities of all authorized institutions remained broadly unchanged, edging down from 56.4% six months earlier to 56.3% (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all authorized institutions The average Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions rose from 89.3% at the end of June 2019 to 90.3% at the end of 2019 (Chart 5.10), as Hong Kong dollar loans and advances remained broadly stable while deposits declined slightly during the review period.67 Meanwhile, as foreign-currency loan growth outpaced deposit growth, the average foreign-currency loan-to-deposit ratio also rose from 58.9% to 60.4% over the same period. Overall, the average loan-to-deposit ratio in all currencies of all authorized institutions rose from 74.5% at the end of June 2019 to 75.4% at the end of the year.
