Given that the Aggregate Balance of the banking system had remained stable since April 2019 and deposits were broadly steady, there were no clear signs of substantial fund outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system during the review period. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of all authorized institutions The interest rate risk exposures of locally incorporated licensed banks remained relatively low in the fourth quarter of 2019. We estimate that, assuming a shock of a 200-basis-point increase in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would be equivalent to 1.56% of their total capital base at the end of 2019 (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Impact of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks Against the backdrop of China-US trade tensions, a slowdown in the global economy and persistent local social incidents, bank credit growth slowed in the second half of 2019 after a moderate rebound in the first half. On a half-yearly basis, loan growth, as measured by the change in total loans and advances of all authorized institutions, increased moderately by 4.2% in the first half of 2019 before slowing to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The slowdown in loan growth was attributable to slower growth in both domestic loans, comprising loans for use in Hong Kong and trade finance, and loans for use outside Hong Kong during the review period. Domestic loans and loans for use outside Hong Kong grew by 2.5% and 2.2% respectively in the second half of 2019, lower than the increases of 4.5% and 3.5% in the first half. Nevertheless, growth in total loans for 2019 as a whole increased moderately to 6.7%, from 4.4% for 2018 as a whole.

The rollout of coronavirus vaccines brought hope of reopening economies and boosted the global growth outlook. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing, financial markets repeatedly reached new highs. However, uncertainty continued to cloud the global outlook, and the pace of recovery was expected to vary across economies. Over the medium term, the disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, elevated debt levels and lasting economic scars from the pandemic will pose challenges for policymakers. The Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and orderly. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level, mainly driven by equity-related demand. During the review period, total deposits increased, with no signs of significant fund outflows from the local banking system. Partly reflecting subdued economic activity and lower credit demand amid recurring outbreaks, total loans in the banking sector declined slightly in the second half of the year, although a modest increase was still recorded for 2020 as a whole. Meanwhile, the residential property market remained broadly stable. Looking ahead, uncertainty surrounding the pace of economic recovery and persistent geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges to the local banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic may weaken the debt-servicing capacity of corporates and households, the banking sector should remain vigilant to the impact of the relevant downside risk factors on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies reopened, but slowed again from the fourth quarter as coronavirus infections resurged. Nevertheless, breakthroughs in vaccine development towards the end of 2020 raised market expectations that the pandemic would eventually come to an end, facilitating a return of the global economy to normality and an acceleration in growth. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing, global financial markets reached new highs in early 2021, even as signs of a disconnect from the real economy began to emerge. Against this backdrop, uncertainty will continue to cloud the global economic outlook. It remains to be seen whether vaccines can be widely distributed. Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks and earlier aggressive easing policies could lead to higher-than-expected inflation, prompting central banks to reduce monetary accommodation earlier and ending financial markets’ expectations of a “lower-for-longer” monetary policy stance. Over the longer term, policymakers will need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures and address the many economic legacies of the pandemic, including elevated global debt levels and lasting economic scars. In East Asia, domestic gross domestic product growth improved in the second half of 2020, supported by a recovery in export demand. Amid increased risk appetite, portfolio investment inflows into the region rebounded and the search for yield re-emerged. Despite these positive developments, East Asia continued to face persistent uncertainty arising from the pandemic. First, in the global competition for vaccine procurement, the region’s less developed economies may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hindering the recovery of their tourism and service sectors. Second, uncertainties over vaccine supply, coverage or efficacy, together with weakening government fiscal positions in the region, could dampen market sentiment and trigger a reversal of capital flows. In Mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually returned to normal. For 2020 as a whole, the Mainland economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook will continue to depend largely on the development of the pandemic and changes in China-US tensions. The latest consensus forecast indicated that the Mainland economy would grow by 8.4% in 2021. The renminbi depreciated for several months at the beginning of 2020, before strengthening over the remainder of the year as the economic recovery accelerated, the US dollar weakened and the Mainland bond market recorded strong capital inflows. A detailed study shows that during the coronavirus outbreak, fundamental factors rather than market sentiment played a more important role in driving fluctuations in the renminbi exchange rate (see Box 1 for details). The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real gross domestic product remained well below its pre-pandemic level. With a modest increase in domestic demand and a further expansion in merchandise exports, seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product began to recover in the third quarter, ending five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real gross domestic product also narrowed markedly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to around 3% in the second half. However, for 2020 as a whole, real gross domestic product fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record and, following a 1.2% contraction in 2019, the first consecutive annual declines in history. The latest gross domestic product data by sector showed that consumption- and tourism-related sectors contracted more severely than the overall economy during the pandemic. In response to the ongoing pandemic, the Government introduced two further rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund in the second half of 2020 to assist sectors and members of the public affected by the pandemic and enhance Hong Kong’s anti-epidemic capability. The Government also announced additional countercyclical measures to boost the economy in the recent 2021/22 Budget, including a one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption voucher and a 100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme for unemployed persons. In March 2021, the HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, also announced that the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme would be extended to October of the same year, as well as an extension of the repayment period for trade facilities under the Scheme. These extension measures were expected to help alleviate the cash flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. Coronavirus vaccines hold out the prospect of a return to normal economic activity, and the local economy was expected to resume positive growth in 2021 as a whole. However, the strength and pace of the recovery were subject to numerous uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the pace and effectiveness of the vaccine rollout. As widespread vaccination would take time, the local economy would continue to face significant challenges in early 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy was expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong’s exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies would depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes. The Government forecast real gross domestic product growth of between 3.5–5.5% in 2021, while the growth forecasts of international organisations and private-sector analysts averaged 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The unemployment rate rose further to a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, while the underemployment rate also climbed to 4.0%, the highest level since the SARS outbreak. In response to the continued deterioration in labour market conditions, the Government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing time-limited wage subsidies (from June to November 2020) to employers to help them retain employees. Following the conclusion of the Employment Support Scheme, the Government introduced other targeted measures (such as one-off subsidies) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to provide further support to sectors hard hit by the pandemic. In the near term, the labour market was expected to remain under pressure amid weak economic conditions. Box 2 examines the potential impact of the rise and fall of inbound tourism on the local labour market. Local inflationary pressures continued to ease during the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. Underlying consumer price inflation fell markedly year on year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and declined further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively. Although the three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, fluctuated slightly in recent months, it also remained at a low level. As global and local economic conditions remained challenging, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong were likely to remain modest in the near term. In particular, local inflation would continue to be contained by the earlier slowdown in newly signed private residential rental growth. The market consensus forecast for headline inflation in 2021 was a moderate 1.4%, while the Government forecast underlying and headline inflation of 1.0% and 1.6% respectively for 2021. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level, mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including that arising from buoyant initial public offering activities and southbound inflows through Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. Fund-raising activities remained active in the first two months of 2021, keeping the Hong Kong dollar strong. During the review period, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, resulting in inflows of HK$263.3 billion into the Hong Kong dollar. For 2020 as a whole, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 85 times, resulting in cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Analysed by geographical location, total deposits increased during the review period, indicating no signs of significant fund outflows from the local banking system. Although uncertainties associated with the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery and persistent China-US tensions could intensify capital flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system and is therefore capable of withstanding such volatility. As the triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking increased the Aggregate Balance, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally remained at very low levels. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funding for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.23% at the end of February 2021. As funding costs declined, the average lending rate for new mortgages also fell from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. On the other hand, the best lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. As the onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rate strengthened, the offshore renminbi (CNH) appreciated against the US dollar from late May 2020. For most of the review period, the offshore renminbi exchange rate traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi exchange rate, with the average premium in the fourth quarter at around 100 pips, which remained moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020, with renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increasing to RMB826.3 billion at the end of January 2021. As for other renminbi business, renminbi bank lending in Hong Kong declined, while renminbi trade settlement increased, and the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high at RMB1,191.5 billion for 2020 as a whole. Hong Kong has an efficient financial infrastructure that provides investors with numerous cross-boundary channels connecting with the Mainland. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business was expected to benefit from the continued opening of the Mainland’s capital account, increasing international investor demand for renminbi assets, and deepening regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives. Supported by rising global equity markets and active purchases of Hong Kong stocks by Mainland investors through Stock Connect, the local equity market rebounded after a sharp correction at the beginning of the review period. Global equity markets rose due to the unprecedented monetary easing measures adopted by major economies; optimism over positive progress in vaccine development, which could help accelerate the recovery in economic activity; and reduced global geopolitical uncertainty. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recouped its losses following a sharp decline in 2020, rising by 15.1% during the review period and at one point surpassing the 31,000-point mark in mid-February 2021, reaching a 32-month high. Supported by steady issuance, the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi bond markets continued to expand in the second half of 2020. Following substantial net fund outflows in the first half of 2020, market confidence recovered rapidly as governments around the world introduced unprecedented economic stimulus measures, and bond fund inflows into the local market rebounded. Although bond yields rose moderately during the same period, global bond yields, including those in Hong Kong, remained near historical lows.

With breakthroughs in vaccine development, the market expected the COVID-19 pandemic to eventually come to an end and global economic growth to accelerate thereafter. Coupled with expectations of a global monetary policy stance of “low interest rates for longer”, investors were not deterred by the resurgence of the pandemic at the end of 2020, and financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021. However, the financial markets’ high expectations were somewhat disconnected from the still-challenging macroeconomic environment. If the economic recovery proved weaker than expected, or policy support was withdrawn earlier than anticipated (for example, because inflation exceeded expectations), asset prices could become volatile. Looking ahead, policymakers would face the difficult question of when to withdraw policy support, as well as having to address the many problems left by the pandemic, including high debt levels and long-term economic scarring. Persistent pandemic-related uncertainties continued to cast a shadow over East Asia’s economic recovery, and the region’s less developed emerging market economies might face greater challenges in vaccine procurement and distribution. Any setbacks in vaccination programmes could reverse the prevailing optimism and destabilise capital inflows and financial markets. In Mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually returned to normal. Looking ahead, the growth outlook remained highly uncertain and would depend largely on the development of the pandemic and changes in China-US tensions. Accordingly, the Government announced that it would maintain a supportive policy stance and emphasised the importance of containing systemic risks. Benefiting from the release of purchasing power following economic reopening, most major economies recorded stronger-than-expected real gross domestic product growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, since the fourth quarter, COVID-19 infections had risen again, prompting governments to reimpose lockdowns and social-distancing measures, and weakening global growth momentum once more. At the end of 2020, more transmissible virus variants emerged and subsequently spread around the world, making the situation more severe. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of several vaccines for use at the end of 2020, the market expected the pandemic to eventually come to an end, with the global economy returning to normal and growth accelerating. Another driver supporting the global economic recovery came from continued policy stimulus, including major central banks’ commitment to a monetary policy stance of “low interest rates for longer” amid subdued inflation, and continued fiscal easing in major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Accordingly, in January 2021, the International Monetary Fund raised its forecast for global gross domestic product growth in 2021 to 5.5%, 0.3 percentage point higher than its forecast made in October 2020 (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real gross domestic product growth forecasts made by the International Monetary Fund in January 2021 and October 2020 Against this backdrop, market optimism strengthened, and share prices of cyclical sectors that typically benefit from economic recovery rose, driving global equity prices and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Chart 2.2). Chart 2.2 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratios of major stock indices However, while financial markets performed strongly, the macroeconomic environment remained challenging, and the disconnect between the two could lead to volatility in asset markets amid multiple risks. First, the prospects for bringing the pandemic under control depended on whether vaccines could be widely distributed, which remained to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, the overall global vaccination rate remained low (Chart 2.3). Although global mechanisms (such as COVAX) promoted more equitable vaccine distribution, limited vaccine supply was expected to make the problem of low vaccination rates in lower-income emerging market economies even more severe. If the pandemic was not brought under control as expected, social-distancing and other restrictive measures might need to be extended, thereby undermining the prospects for global recovery. Chart 2.3 Proportion of the population in selected economies having received at least one vaccine dose (as of 15 March 2021) Second, the financial market rebound was predicated on continued monetary and fiscal policy support, particularly the monetary policy stance of “low interest rates for longer”. However, there was a risk that support measures might be withdrawn faster than expected. For example, amid the combined effects of supply bottlenecks, strong monetary and liquidity growth, and aggressive fiscal easing, inflation expectations in the US and Europe had already risen (Chart 2.4). If future inflation was stronger than expected, central banks might need to scale back monetary easing, while higher-than-expected inflation data could also lead to greater financial market volatility. Chart 2.4 US and euro-area 5-year/5-year inflation-linked swap rates Third, significant uncertainty surrounded future China-US relations. The wave of China-US “decoupling”, particularly in the financial and technology sectors, had intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. Given the increasingly hardline stance towards Mainland China among both Democrats and Republicans in the US, this trend might not be reversed under the Biden administration. An unexpected escalation in China-US tensions could trigger financial market turmoil in the future. Looking ahead, policymakers would need to confront the difficult question of whether and when to withdraw pandemic support measures. While withdrawing such measures too early could jeopardise the economic recovery and create a “cliff effect”, these measures would be costly in the long run, including by creating fiscal burdens and delaying the post-pandemic reallocation of resources that was necessary, such as allowing “zombie companies” whose business models were no longer viable to survive with continued government support. In addition, policymakers would also need to address the many problems left by the pandemic. First, owing to declines in corporate revenue and surging government expenditure, global debt levels rose sharply in 2020 (Chart 2.5). Although the problems arising from the sharp rise in debt might not be imminent because global interest rates were currently extremely low, continued debt accumulation in the public and private sectors could raise market concerns about fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Chart 2.5 Global debt as a percentage of gross domestic product Another lingering problem involved the potential long-term economic losses or lasting scarring caused by the pandemic. For example, elevated uncertainty might lead businesses to reduce investment, while workers suffering prolonged unemployment might permanently leave the labour market, resulting in a substantial waste of human resources. In East Asia, after a sharp decline in the second quarter of 2020, real gross domestic product growth stabilised in the second half of the year (Chart 2.6). The economic recovery was driven mainly by a rebound in exports, with particularly strong export demand for electronic and technological equipment. Meanwhile, the hardest-hit service sectors, such as tourism and consumer services requiring face-to-face customer contact, remained under strain. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Real gross domestic product growth in 2020 Despite lingering uncertainties over the economic recovery, portfolio investment funds had begun to flow back into the region. Since the second half of last year, improved market sentiment and higher yields relative to advanced-economy bonds had attracted more bond fund inflows into the region (Chart 2.7). As signs of economic recovery emerged and vaccine production programmes were launched, equity fund inflows into East Asia also accelerated in the final quarter of 2020. Regional currencies appreciated accordingly amid portfolio fund inflows, with the Bloomberg JPMorgan Asia Dollar Index rebounding by about 10% from its low in March last year. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Portfolio investment fund flows East Asia continued to face persistent pandemic-related uncertainties. First, although the rollout of vaccines brought hope to the region’s hardest-hit service sectors and economies, global competition for early batches of vaccines drove up procurement costs, while vaccine distribution also posed challenges to the region’s logistics and public health capacity. As a result, the region’s less developed economies might achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, while uneven vaccination across economies could prolong border closures and delay the recovery of tourism-related sectors. Second, as investor optimism was largely driven by vaccine rollouts, if the progress or effectiveness of vaccination fell far short of expectations, the prevailing capital inflows and rebound in financial asset prices could come to an end. A sudden decline in capital inflows could trigger another wave of market turmoil. With COVID-19 successfully brought under control and consumption gradually recovering, the Mainland economy rebounded rapidly in the second half of 2020. At the same time, exports continued to grow, benefiting from strong demand for pandemic-related products, such as medical supplies and high-tech products (Chart 2.8). For 2020 as a whole, despite the unprecedented shock to the economy from the COVID-19 pandemic, Mainland gross domestic product still grew by 2.3%. Chart 2.8 Mainland China: Contributions of demand components to gross domestic product growth Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecast indicated that the Mainland economy would grow strongly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to become the main driver of economic growth. However, whether the economic recovery could be sustained would still depend to some extent on the development of the pandemic. Although industrial production activities in the Mainland had normalised, the service sector remained partially disrupted following renewed outbreaks in several northern provinces. Regarding the external environment, although exports resumed growth in the second half of 2020, global demand remained uncertain because of new waves of the pandemic in most developed economies. In addition, China-US tensions might not ease in the short term, but the recently signed Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement and the agreed Comprehensive Agreement on Investment between China and the EU would help further integrate China with other economies and might partly offset the adverse impact of China-US decoupling on the economic recovery. Given that the economic outlook remained highly uncertain, the Government announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that there would be no major change in the existing policy stance in 2021, in order to support economic growth, while also emphasising the importance of containing systemic risks, such as maintaining the stability of macro leverage and the sustainability of local government debt. In addition, the latest Government Work Report set the growth target for 2021 at above 6%. Over the longer term, the 14th Five-Year Plan designated technological self-reliance and the dual circulation strategy, among others, as development priorities, with the aim of raising per capita gross domestic product to the level of moderately developed countries by 2035. The impact of the COVID-19 outbreak on bond issuers’ repayment capacity appeared limited, and the overall default rate in the Mainland bond market remained low in the second half of 2020. However, owing to a sharp rise in defaults on bonds issued by state-owned enterprises, the total amount of defaulted bonds increased in 2020 (Chart 2.9). Although the rise in defaults by state-owned enterprises mainly reflected the Central Government’s determination to break the “rigid repayment” expectation for state-owned enterprises in order to promote more rational market risk pricing, limited fiscal space among some local governments, particularly those in less developed regions, might also have been a factor. Chart 2.9 Mainland China: Scale and ratio of onshore bond defaults In the second half of 2020, financing costs for corporate issuers increased, particularly for some high-risk issuers. Although the continued economic recovery and gradual normalisation of interest rates contributed to some extent to higher financing costs for lower-rated issuers, several corporate defaults in the final quarter of 2020 led to a marked widening of credit spreads (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 Mainland China: 5-year corporate bond yields Regarding the property market, Mainland housing prices continued to rise in the second half of 2020, particularly in first-tier cities. By contrast, housing prices in lower-tier cities rose much more slowly (Chart 2.11). The problem of housing oversupply that had troubled third-tier cities in previous years was largely brought under control in 2020, partly because third-tier cities recorded strong sales amid buoyant market sentiment. As of the end of 2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio in third-tier cities remained at around 13 months, well below the peak of 31 months in early 2015.

Although real Gross Domestic Product remained well below its pre-pandemic level, the Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 as domestic demand recovered and exports of goods expanded further. With expectations that COVID-19 vaccination would enable economic activity to return to normal, the local economy was expected to resume growth in 2021 after recording its most severe contraction on record in 2020. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery were subject to numerous uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of the vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination would take time, the local economy would still face considerable challenges in early 2021. The labour market was therefore expected to remain under pressure in the near term, while domestic inflationary pressures would remain mild. The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), although economic activity remained well below its pre-pandemic level. The year-on-year decline in real Gross Domestic Product narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. For 2020 as a whole, however, real Gross Domestic Product fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record and, following a contraction of 1.2% in 2019, the first-ever decline for two consecutive years. The latest Gross Domestic Product data by industry also showed that economic activity in the vast majority of industries recorded year-on-year declines in recent quarters, with consumer- and tourism-related industries contracting more sharply than the overall economy. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, real Gross Domestic Product began to recover from the third quarter of 2020, ending five consecutive quarters of decline (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). Local private consumption returned to positive growth in the third and fourth quarters. However, amid the third and fourth local waves of the pandemic, the authorities reimposed social distancing measures, and consumer confidence remained weak. Overall investment expenditure also increased in the second half of the year as business sentiment improved briefly. Partly benefiting from stronger export performance, particularly exports to Mainland China, Hong Kong’s trade in goods expanded further (Chart 3.2). Trade in services remained weak as global tourism remained at a standstill. Overall, net imports (the trade deficit) dragged down Gross Domestic Product in the second half of the year, partly reflecting a slower recovery in exports of goods than in imports. Chart 3.1 Real Gross Domestic Product growth and contributions from major expenditure components Chart 3.2 Exports and imports in real terms In response to the persistent pandemic, the Government launched two further rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund totalling HK$30.4 billion between September and December 2020 to assist industries and members of the public affected by the pandemic and enhance Hong Kong’s anti-epidemic capability. The Government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to boost the economy, including the issuance of one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption vouchers and the provision of 100% guaranteed personal concessionary loans to unemployed persons. In March 2021, the HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, also announced a further extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October of the same year and an extension of the repayment period for trade facilities under the Scheme. These extension measures were expected to help alleviate the cash-flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. COVID-19 vaccines offered hope that economic activity would return to normal, and the Hong Kong economy was expected to resume positive growth in 2021 as a whole. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery were subject to numerous uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of the vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination would take time, the local economy would still face considerable challenges in the early part of 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy was expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong’s exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies would depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes, thereby affecting Hong Kong’s trade in goods and inbound tourism. The Government forecast real Gross Domestic Product growth of 3.5–5.5% for 2021 as a whole, while the growth forecasts of international organisations and private-sector analysts averaged 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose further to 7.2% in February 2021, a 17-year high (Chart 3.3). The underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, the highest level since the SARS outbreak. Total employment stabilised after falling to a low level (Chart 3.3), while Government figures showed that the number of job vacancies continued to decline. The year-on-year growth of the Nominal Index of Payroll per Person Engaged, which reflects labour earnings, slowed to 2.0% in the third quarter of 2020, the lowest in nearly 11 years. In response to the continued deterioration in labour market conditions, the Government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund to provide employers with time-limited wage subsidies (from June to November 2020) to help them retain employees. Following the end of the Employment Support Scheme, the Government introduced other targeted measures, such as one-off subsidies, under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to provide further support to industries hard hit by the pandemic. In the near term, the labour market was expected to remain under pressure because of weak economic conditions. Box 2 examines the potential impact of the rise and fall of inbound tourism on the local labour market. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Chart 3.4 Different indicators of consumer price inflation Domestic inflationary pressures continued to ease over the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. Underlying consumer price inflation fell markedly year on year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively (Chart 3.4). Although the three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, fluctuated slightly in recent months, it also remained low. Specifically, price pressures for basic food eased, while the cost of meals bought away from home declined noticeably, reflecting the take-away discounts offered by more restaurants while dine-in services were restricted. Price pressures for other tradable goods, such as durable goods, remained moderate. On the services front, the rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index remained weak as private residential rents consolidated (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures also eased in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.5 Rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index and market rents Chart 3.6 Unit labour costs As global and domestic economic conditions remained challenging, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong should remain mild in the near term. In particular, domestic inflation would continue to be restrained by the earlier slowdown in the growth of newly contracted private residential rents. The market consensus forecast an overall inflation rate of a moderate 1.4% in 2021, while the Government forecast an underlying inflation rate of 1% and an overall inflation rate of 1.6% for 2021. As the COVID-19 pandemic raged, inbound tourism rapidly fell into a depression, raising market concerns that the crisis would have scarring effects on the subsequent labour market recovery. To this end, this Box empirically analyses the impact of booming inbound tourism on Hong Kong’s labour market, thereby examining the potential implications of the current tourism depression. Inbound tourism has experienced major ups and downs since 2000 (Chart B2.1). Specifically, visitor arrivals declined during the 2003 outbreak of SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome). Visitor arrivals began to surge following the launch of the Individual Visit Scheme (IVS) in July of that year. Under the original IVS, Mainland residents could apply as individuals to visit Hong Kong once or twice a year, with each stay not exceeding 7 days. The IVS was expanded from April 2009 to allow eligible residents with Shenzhen household registration to apply for multiple-entry Individual Visit endorsements valid for one year (multiple-entry permits). Mainland visitor arrivals increased substantially thereafter. Driven by new cross-boundary infrastructure linking Hong Kong and Mainland China, visitor arrivals reached an all-time high from late 2018 to early 2019. Subsequent local social incidents halved visitor arrivals in the second half of 2019, while inbound tourism had been at a standstill since late January 2020 amid the COVID-19 pandemic. Chart B2.1 Visitor arrivals and related policies Taking the tourism boom brought about by the IVS as an example, we examine the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and earnings. We regard the introduction of the IVS in 2003 as akin to a random economic shock because its timing was nearly exogenous and its introduction could not have been anticipated by Hong Kong residents. The main data for our analysis are population data from Hong Kong’s Population Censuses or By-censuses. Specifically, we use the 5% samples from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011 and 2016 Population Censuses or By-censuses. We also define the tourism-related industries as the food and beverage, retail, hotel and transport industries. First, we employ a difference-in-differences framework to compare differences in employment outcomes before and after the implementation of the IVS between younger workers (aged 20-40) in the treatment group and older workers (aged 41-65) in the comparison group. We classify the younger cohort as the treatment group because they were still at an early stage of their careers and could therefore make major changes to their employment choices more flexibly in response to the exogenous growth in inbound tourism. As the labour market impact of the tourism boom brought about by the IVS could vary over time, we also employ an event study to identify time-varying effects. Our empirical results show that, compared with the older cohort, younger workers, particularly women and workers with only secondary education, were more likely to enter tourism-related industries after the implementation of the IVS. In particular, the effect of the IVS on the probability of younger women working in tourism-related industries was especially significant and persistent, remaining close to 5 percentage points from 2006 onwards in terms of the average difference in entry probability relative to the older cohort (Chart B2.2). We also use a similar approach to compare the earnings of workers in tourism-related industries (the treatment group) with those in non-tourism-related industries (the comparison group). The estimation results show that, following the implementation of the IVS, workers in tourism-related industries experienced higher earnings growth than employees in non-tourism-related industries. Moreover, compared with similar employees in other industries, female workers and workers with lower educational attainment in tourism-related industries recorded larger and increasing earnings gains (3-20 percentage points) (Chart B2.3). Chart B2.2 Impact of the IVS on female employment Chart B2.3 Impact of the IVS on the earnings of women and workers with lower educational attainment The above results are broadly consistent with international experience, revealing that tourism is an important source of employment, particularly for young people, women and workers with lower educational attainment. In Hong Kong’s case, our findings are also consistent with previous analyses that the strong growth of inbound tourism increased market demand for lower-skilled workers and improved the resilience of the lower-skilled segment of the labour market. As inbound tourism falls from boom to trough, these groups of workers may be more severely affected and warrant close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate continued to stay close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level, with the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking being triggered multiple times between September and October 2020. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including buoyant initial public offering activities and southbound fund flows through Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. As the Aggregate Balance increased to over HK$450 billion, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates declined across the board. Although uncertainties related to developments in the COVID-19 pandemic, the pace of economic recovery and persistent China-US tensions may exacerbate fund flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, enabling it to withstand pressures arising from such volatility. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate stayed close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level, mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including buoyant initial public offering activities and southbound fund flows through Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.1). Although some proceeds raised from initial public offerings were remitted out, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate traded within a narrow range of 7.7505–7.7544 in November and December amid improved sentiment in the local stock market and market expectations of increased funding demand towards the end of the year. As fund-raising activities remained active in the first two months of 2021 (Chart 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar closed at 7.7568 against the US dollar on 26 February 2021. Overall, trading of the Hong Kong dollar continued to be smooth and orderly. During the review period, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered multiple times, resulting in an increase in the Aggregate Balance and reflecting substantial inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. In September and October 2020, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 47 times. In accordance with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System, the HKMA sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, increasing the Aggregate Balance from HK$193.1 billion at end-August to HK$457.5 billion at end-February (Chart 4.3). The strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered a total of 85 times in 2020, with cumulative inflows amounting to HK$383.5 billion. From a cross-border perspective, total deposits increased, indicating no signs of substantial fund outflows from the local banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments figures showed that direct investment by non-residents continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, with no indication of any unusual fund movements. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Equity funds raised on Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX) Chart 4.3 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes During the review period, the nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar declined broadly in line with the weakening of the US dollar against major currencies (Chart 4.4). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar, the latter broadly tracked the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.4 Nominal and real effective exchange rates Looking ahead, uncertainties related to developments in the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery and persistent China-US tensions may exacerbate fund flow volatility. As an international financial centre, Hong Kong hosts various fund-raising activities, such as initial public offerings, resulting in substantial fund inflows and outflows. On the one hand, such fund-raising activities may attract international investors to transfer funds to Hong Kong. On the other hand, funds raised by listed companies may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong for business purposes. Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, enabling it to withstand fund flow volatility without affecting financial stability. Amid continued inflows into the Hong Kong dollar, local monetary conditions remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. Over the eight months since end-June 2020, the Hong Kong dollar monetary base increased by 20.8% (Chart 4.5). By component, the increase in the monetary base during the period reflected the rise in the Aggregate Balance resulting from the multiple triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking. Other components, including Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the monetary base During the review period, large-scale initial public offering activities increased Hong Kong dollar deposits arising from initial public offering subscription loans. As a result, Hong Kong dollar broad money (Hong Kong dollar M3) and its Hong Kong dollar deposit component rose significantly from July to October 2020 and in January 2021 (Chart 4.6). Following the completion of initial public offering activities and the repayment of initial public offering subscription loans by customers, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels at the end of 2020. In January 2021, Hong Kong dollar M3 again increased substantially, mainly driven by a large-scale initial public offering at the end of January. Overall, over the seven months since end-June, Hong Kong dollar M3 grew by 21.7%; excluding the impact of the initial public offering at the end of January, Hong Kong dollar M3 grew moderately by 9.1%. According to an analysis of counterpart assets, excluding initial public offering subscription loans, the growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 was mainly attributable to the increase in the monetary base driven by the triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking (Chart 4.7). As the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits increased by 22.9% over the same period; excluding the impact of the initial public offering at the end of January, Hong Kong dollar deposits grew moderately by 9.1%. Although Hong Kong dollar time deposits declined because of low deposit rates, this was more than fully offset by rapid growth in demand and savings deposits driven partly by investment demand. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions by currency Chart 4.7 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and counterpart assets Total foreign currency deposits grew steadily by 3.6% over the seven months since end-June. US dollar deposits edged down by 0.3%, partly reflecting the weakness of the US dollar, while other foreign currency deposits grew strongly by 15.5% over the same period, mainly reflecting an increase in renminbi deposits. Overall, owing to short-term fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar deposits caused by initial public offering activities, total deposits with authorized institutions increased substantially by 13.2% during the review period (Chart 4.6). Excluding the initial public offering at the end of January, total deposits grew moderately by 6.4%. It should be noted that monthly monetary statistics may fluctuate because of various short-term factors, such as seasonal and initial-public-offering-related funding demand, as well as business- and investment-related activities, and should therefore be interpreted with caution. As the Aggregate Balance increased, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally remained at very low levels during the review period (Chart 4.8). Despite large-scale initial public offering activities in the second half of 2020, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates did not fluctuate substantially because of ample liquidity in the banking system. Overall, the local interbank market continued to function normally. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve broadly tracked movements in the US dollar yield curve and steepened during the review period, with short-term bond yields declining and long-term bond yields rising (Chart 4.9). Compared with end-June, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong Government Bonds edged down by 4 basis points to 0.23% at end-February, while the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds rose by 67 basis points to 1.30% over the same period. Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, composite interest rate and average interest rate on new mortgage loans Hong Kong dollar interest rates at the retail level mainly declined in line with Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at end-June to 0.23% at end-February 2021 (Chart 4.9). As funding costs declined, the average interest rate on new mortgage loans also fell from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in January 2021, broadly tracking the 1-month Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rate. Meanwhile, retail banks’ best lending rates remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are influenced by US dollar interest rates. Given the prolonged low interest rate environment in the United States, Hong Kong dollar interest rates should remain low, with occasional fluctuations due to capital market activities and seasonal liquidity demand. In the face of a highly uncertain macro-financial environment, ample liquidity in the banking system should provide a sufficient buffer to maintain Hong Kong’s monetary and financial stability. The offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rates against the US dollar strengthened from end-May (Chart 4.10), broadly reflecting the more favourable economic outlook for Mainland China compared with the rest of the world, as well as the weakness of the US dollar. FTSE Russell’s announcement at end-September that Mainland government bonds would be included in the World Government Bond Index further supported the strengthening of the renminbi through investment demand. For most of the review period, the offshore renminbi exchange rate traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi exchange rate, averaging about 100 points in the fourth quarter, which remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates During the review period, liquidity conditions in the offshore renminbi interbank market remained stable. Although the overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate experienced brief fluctuations owing to occasional northbound remittance demand and seasonal liquidity demand towards the end of the year, it remained below 4% most of the time (Chart 4.11). The 3-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate declined in late December in line with onshore renminbi interest rates, before rising again in late January, partly because of tighter onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. Chart 4.11 Overnight and 3-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate fixings In the second half of 2020, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to grow. Since the fourth quarter, growth in renminbi deposits accelerated, reflecting to some extent the appreciation of the renminbi and its higher interest rates relative to other currencies. Compared with end-June 2020, the combined balance of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew at a faster pace, reaching RMB826.3 billion at end-January 2021, an increase of 21.9% (Chart 4.12 and Table 4.A). Of this, renminbi customer deposits grew by 24.7%, mainly driven by strong growth in corporate customer deposits. Meanwhile, the outstanding amount of certificates of deposit decreased by 25.0% over the same period. Chart 4.12 Renminbi deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong As for other renminbi business, outstanding renminbi loans declined by 2.4% to RMB159.2 billion over the seven months since end-June 2020. Meanwhile, renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow strongly. During the seven months from July 2020 to January 2021, transactions handled by banks in Hong Kong reached RMB3,769.5 billion, an increase of 16.7% over the same period a year earlier. Among these transactions, remittances from Hong Kong to the Mainland increased more than remittances from the Mainland to Hong Kong (Chart 4.13). Hong Kong has a large renminbi liquidity pool, sufficient to continue supporting a substantial volume of renminbi payments and financial transactions. In 2020, the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system reached RMB1,191.5 billion, compared with RMB1,133.9 billion in 2019.

As the recurring coronavirus pandemic prolonged the economic recession, coupled with the impact of the prolonged low interest rate environment, the profitability of Hong Kong’s retail banks declined further in the second half of 2020, while asset quality also deteriorated slightly. Nevertheless, Hong Kong’s banking sector remained sound, underpinned by its continued strong capital and liquidity positions. During the review period, the HKMA decided to extend a number of relief measures to continue supporting the overall economy through the difficult period. Looking ahead, although the rollout of vaccines may raise hopes that the global pandemic can be brought under control and economic activity can resume, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. These uncertainties and persistent geopolitical tensions will weigh on business activity and continue to pose challenges to Hong Kong’s banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic will weaken the repayment capacity of corporates and households, the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impact of the related downside risk factors on its asset quality. In the second half of 2020, retail banks’ aggregate pre-tax operating profit fell by 38.5% compared with the same period in 2019. Correspondingly, return on assets declined to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, compared with 1.13% in the same period in 2019 (Chart 5.1). The net interest margin of retail banks narrowed from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 to 1.01% in the same period of 2020 (Chart 5.2), resulting in a decline in net interest income that outweighed the slight increase in non-interest income and thereby reduced profitability. For 2020 as a whole, retail banks’ aggregate pre-tax operating profit fell by 29.4%, while return on assets declined from 1.19% in 2019 to 0.77%. Chart 5.1 Retail banks’ profitability Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Largely driven by substantial fund inflows arising from stock market activities, Hong Kong dollar liquidity became more abundant. The Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. In particular, the 3-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate fell by 43 basis points in the second half of the year to 0.35% at end-2020 (blue line in Chart 5.3). The Composite Interest Rate (a measure of retail banks’ average cost of Hong Kong dollar funding) followed a broadly similar trend, declining markedly from 0.71% at end-June 2020 to 0.28% at end-2020 (green line in Chart 5.3). The decline in the Composite Interest Rate mainly reflected lower interbank funding costs and reductions in time deposit rates by some major retail banks. Chart 5.3 Interest rates From a broader perspective, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost of locally licensed banks fell moderately by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturity of licensed banks Looking ahead, the profitability outlook for the banking sector will remain challenging, as the global low interest rate environment is likely to persist and continue to adversely affect banks’ net interest margins. In addition, despite breakthroughs in vaccine development that have strengthened market optimism about the global economic outlook, the trajectory of economic recovery remains highly uncertain, given the considerable uncertainties surrounding vaccine distribution and efficacy. These risk factors will continue to affect the banking sector’s loan quality and profitability in the near term. The Hong Kong banking sector remained well capitalised, with capital levels far above the minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorised institutions was 20.7% at end-December 2020, above the international minimum requirement of 8% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio was 18.7% during the period, of which 16.7% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorised institutions remained at a sound level of 8.2% at end-December 2020, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated authorised institutions Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorised institutions As measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement under Basel III, the banking sector’s liquidity position remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. During the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions was 57.9%, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The latest ratios under the Net Stable Funding Ratio requirement also indicated stable funding positions among authorised institutions. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions and the average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained at high levels of 138.6% and 139.5%, respectively, in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.8), well above their respective statutory minimum requirements of 100% and 75%. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of authorised institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the main source of funding for authorised institutions, reflecting the stable funding structure maintained by the banking system. At end-2020, customer deposits accounted for 56.1% of the total liabilities of all authorised institutions, similar to the level six months earlier (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all authorised institutions As the total deposits of all authorised institutions increased in the second half of 2020 while total loans declined during the same period, the average all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorised institutions fell from 76.0% at end-June 2020 to 72.3% at end-2020 (Chart 5.10). The increase in total deposits broadly reflected growth in both Hong Kong dollar deposits and foreign currency deposits. Correspondingly, at end-2020, the average Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio and foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined to 83.5% and 61.0%, respectively, compared with 86.4% and 65.5%, respectively, six months earlier. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorised institutions The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained relatively low in the fourth quarter of 2020. Under a hypothetical shock of a 200-basis-point increase in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the estimated decline in the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions would be equivalent to 1.41% of their total capital base at end-December 2020 (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Impact of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks Against the backdrop of a prolonged economic recession caused by the recurring pandemic and tightened social distancing measures, total loans and advances declined moderately in the second half of 2020. Nevertheless, for 2020 as a whole, total credit in the banking sector still recorded positive growth, although the growth rate slowed markedly from 6.7% in 2019 to 1.2%. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all authorised institutions decreased by 1.8% in the second half of 2020 after growing by 3.0% in the first half (Chart 5.12). The decline in total loans was attributable to decreases in both domestic loans (including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade finance) and loans for use outside Hong Kong. In particular, total domestic loans edged down by 0.9% in the second half of the year, while total loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.9%, compared with growth of 2.6% and 4.2%, respectively, during the preceding six months. Chart 5.12 Loan growth Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans remained broadly at the same level at end-2020 as at end-June, after declining by 2.0% in the first half of the year. After surging by 10.6% in the first half of 2020, foreign currency loans decreased by 4.5% in the second half, partly reflecting lower demand for US dollar loans as global liquidity conditions improved. The banking sector became slightly more optimistic about the near-term outlook for credit demand than six months earlier. The HKMA’s December 2020 Survey on Credit Condition Outlook showed that the proportion of respondent authorised institutions expecting loan demand to increase over the next three months rose to 37%, while the proportion expecting loan demand to decrease over the same period fell to 13% (Table 5.A). As the pandemic adversely affected the repayment capacity of households and corporates, banks’ loan quality deteriorated slightly, but remained sound by historical and international standards. Moreover, the pace of deterioration in loan quality also slowed in the second half of 2020. The gross classified loan ratio of all authorised institutions rose moderately from 0.79% six months earlier to 0.9% at end-2020, while the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio of all authorised institutions increased from 0.49% at end-June 2020 to 0.57% at end-2020. For retail banks, the gross classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio rose to 0.82% and 0.48%, respectively (Chart 5.13).

Entering 2022, the global economy remained weak, while inflationary pressures continued to intensify across regions, particularly in the United States. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties, including the risk of large-scale outbreaks of the pandemic and the possibility that monetary policy tightening may be more aggressive than expected if US inflation proves more persistent and broad-based than anticipated. If the Federal Reserve substantially tightens monetary policy and causes global financial conditions to tighten, the recovery of more vulnerable emerging market economies would come under pressure. More recently, the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may have significant implications for the global economy through trade and financial channels, and further complicate the global monetary policy outlook. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, but trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no significant signs of fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. For 2021 as a whole, growth in total bank lending accelerated. Meanwhile, the residential property market has softened since mid-2021. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may threaten the continued economic recovery, while the normalisation of US monetary policy may proceed faster than expected. These risk factors will pose challenges to banks’ credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of the relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The global economy began to slow in late 2021, with the weakness continuing into 2022, as the spread of the highly contagious Omicron variant led to increased restrictions on mobility worldwide, while persistent supply bottlenecks continued to weigh on production. Meanwhile, amid supply-demand imbalances and labour shortages, global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and broadened to a wide range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the United States. More recently, following the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine, surging commodity prices may further exacerbate the threat of global inflation, while heightened financial market volatility may lead to an undesirable tightening of global financial conditions, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook is subject to significant uncertainty. In the short term, large-scale outbreaks of the pandemic could lead to the reimposition of lockdowns and a renewed deterioration in supply bottlenecks. In the United States, as the risk of inflation being more persistent and broad-based than expected has grown, the Federal Reserve has turned hawkish, accelerating its timetable for tapering asset purchases and raising interest rates, and has begun discussing balance sheet reduction. If the Federal Reserve needs to tighten monetary policy substantially, global financial conditions may also tighten, leading to a deterioration in borrowers’ debt-servicing capacity, while disorderly capital outflows would put pressure on the recovery of relatively vulnerable emerging market economies. More recently, the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may expose global commodity prices to the risk of sustained increases, exacerbate shortages of industrial goods, and increase financial market volatility. Heightened market volatility may also trigger redemption pressure on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risk. Box 1 discusses whether swing pricing, a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds, can reduce these funds’ liquidity risk during periods of market stress, as well as the tool’s potential limitations. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, although the renewed imposition of stringent anti-pandemic measures in some Southeast Asian economies in the third quarter temporarily slowed the recovery momentum, while the region’s technology-exporting economies, South Korea and Singapore, continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products. Although the market generally expects a broad-based recovery in emerging Asia in 2022, the region’s near-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, new variants remain a concern, particularly for economies in the region with lower vaccination rates and constrained public health resources. Second, faster policy normalisation by the Federal Reserve could trigger capital outflows from the region and intensify currency depreciation pressures. Economies in the region that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policies to support economic recovery will face a more difficult trade-off between containing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity. Third, slower growth in major economies, coupled with a possible shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, will weigh on the outlook for trade growth. Fourth, increases in a range of commodity prices triggered by the conflict between Russia and Ukraine will feed through to regional inflation while weakening consumption. Together with increased global economic uncertainty, this will complicate regional central banks’ decisions on monetary policy normalisation. Central banks in some regional economies with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. Over the longer term, to rebuild sustainable and resilient growth models, investors need to attach greater importance to environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 examines the sensitivity of equity returns to changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is affected by companies’ environmental performance. Economic growth in Mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing measures and tightening measures in the property market. Looking ahead, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure in the near term owing to the persistent property market downturn and the outbreak of the Omicron variant. The Mainland authorities have therefore made growth stabilisation their top priority this year and introduced a series of fiscal and monetary support measures. Both total onshore bond defaults and onshore bond defaults by state-owned enterprises decreased in the second half of 2021. Box 3 discusses whether the pricing of state-owned enterprise bonds has improved in recent years. Overall risks in the banking sector remain manageable, as Mainland banks, particularly systemically important banks, have limited exposure to loans to developers, low non-performing loan ratios and high provision coverage ratios. The Hong Kong economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, albeit at a slower pace than in the first half. Seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product grew moderately, as exports of goods and private consumption benefited from the continued global economic recovery, improved local labour market conditions and the Government’s launch of the Consumption Voucher Scheme. On a year-on-year basis, the economy grew by 5.1% in the second half of 2021, compared with 7.8% in the first half. For 2021 as a whole, the economy grew by 6.4%, its first full-year positive growth since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local infections and the resulting tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on Hong Kong’s economic activity. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional countercyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the 100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme and various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme will be enhanced, with maximum loan amounts increased and application and repayment periods extended. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, also extended the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to the end of October 2022. The Scheme also offers borrowers a one-year partial principal repayment option, which is also applicable to loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. The Hong Kong economy is expected to continue recovering in 2022 as a whole, but at a slower pace than in 2021, partly reflecting slower global growth amid the continuing pandemic and a higher base effect. In particular, Hong Kong’s exports of goods will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The Government’s promotion of a number of capital works and infrastructure projects will also support the economy. The Government forecasts real gross domestic product growth of between 2.0% and 3.5% in 2022, while the average growth forecast of international organisations and private-sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to the uncertainties and risks discussed in the preceding sections, particularly the pandemic and the pace of US monetary policy normalisation. As the economy recovered, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% at year-end. Total employment rebounded but remained below its pre-pandemic level. In early 2022, official data indicated that labour market pressures had re-emerged amid a new wave of local infections. In addition, the decline in the number of online job advertisements also reflected a reduction in new vacancies. The new wave of local infections and tightened anti-pandemic measures will put some pressure on the local labour market in the near term, particularly in sectors involving face-to-face contact. Over the longer term, labour market conditions will depend on local pandemic developments and the pace of the local economic recovery. Local inflationary pressures have generally increased in recent months but remained moderate. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying consumer price inflation rate edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022. The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also picked up in recent months, partly owing to price increases for meals away from home and certain energy-related items. Looking ahead, local inflation is expected to rise slightly in the near term as import prices increase and the pandemic causes logistics disruptions. However, weak rents and moderate local labour cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. The market consensus forecasts headline inflation of 2.4% in 2022, while the Government expects headline inflation of 2.1% and underlying inflation of 2.0% in 2022. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually weakened against the US dollar amid risk-off sentiment in the local stock market. Although the Hong Kong dollar rebounded slightly at one point in October 2021, its appreciation subsequently lost momentum, mainly because of weak southbound net buying through Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect, as well as market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen as the Federal Reserve normalised monetary policy. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar traded on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone most of the time, and trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no significant signs of fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Trading in Hong Kong’s interbank market continued to be smooth and orderly. With ample interbank liquidity, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate remained low during the review period. The average lending rate for new mortgages edged up from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. The best lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Offshore renminbi banking business continued to thrive. In particular, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand, with renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increasing to RMB1,113.5 billion at the end of January 2022. Although outstanding renminbi loans declined, renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system rose to RMB1,522.6 billion in 2021. Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from its efficient financial infrastructure and the two-way, northbound and southbound Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Bond Connect and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect, the continued opening of the Mainland’s capital account, increased demand for renminbi assets from international investors, and deepening regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives. Stimulated by government monetary and fiscal policies, the global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings drove major global equity markets broadly higher in the final quarter of 2021, propelling the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on 4 January 2022. However, growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies amid sharply rising inflation risks, surging commodity prices and escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict have led major global equity markets to consolidate since early January 2022.

Owing to the rapid global spread of virus variants (Delta and Omicron), coupled with persistent production bottlenecks, the global economy slowed markedly in late 2021, and growth momentum remained weak entering 2022. Global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and had spread to a broad range of goods and services in major advanced economies, especially the United States. Growing inflation concerns prompted a hawkish shift in the US Federal Reserve’s monetary policy stance, heightening the risk that premature tightening of global financial conditions could put pressure on currently elevated asset valuations and adversely affect emerging markets, where recoveries generally continued to lag. More recently, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine pushed up energy and other commodity prices and triggered volatility in global financial markets, exacerbating some of the aforementioned risks. In emerging Asia, despite the spread of the Delta variant across the region, the economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, with the region’s major technology-product-exporting economies continuing to outperform other economies. Although the Omicron variant is currently unlikely to seriously impede the region’s economic recovery, any uncertainty associated with new variants will continue to cloud the regional economic outlook. In addition, US Federal Reserve policy normalisation could trigger adjustments in regional asset prices, while slower growth in major economies could weigh on the region’s merchandise export growth. On the one hand, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine has driven up commodity prices and increased inflation risks; on the other hand, it will weaken consumption and increase global economic uncertainty, making monetary policy normalisation decisions more complicated for regional central banks.
