Economic growth in Mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of coronavirus infections, power rationing and measures to tighten the property market. Looking ahead, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure arising from the cooling property market and outbreaks of the Omicron variant. In view of this, the Government has made stabilising growth its top priority this year, and macroeconomic policies will also provide greater support. The global economic recovery slowed visibly in the final quarter of 2021, as the highly transmissible Omicron variant spread on top of the Delta variant, triggering a new wave of infections and leading to tighter mobility restrictions around the world. In addition, supply-chain problems, such as shipping bottlenecks and shortages of key production inputs including semiconductors, continued to constrain production. Entering 2022, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecast in January that global gross domestic product growth would slow from 5.9% in 2021 to 4.4% in 2022, reflecting the persistent drag from the pandemic and supply constraints, reduced policy support in the United States and other major advanced economies, and slowing growth momentum in Mainland China, which offset the expected rebound in growth elsewhere in Asia (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 IMF forecasts of real gross domestic product growth Alongside the slowdown in global economic growth, inflationary pressures continued to increase during the review period. Core inflation (excluding food and energy prices) rose markedly in major advanced economies, particularly the United States, which had adopted larger-scale policy stimulus since the pandemic. Amid supply bottlenecks, the release of pent-up demand and labour shortages, inflationary pressures had spread to a broad range of goods and services (Chart 2.2). In addition, the recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine drove up the prices of a range of commodities and may exacerbate already elevated global inflationary pressures. Chart 2.2 Core Consumer Price Index inflation in selected economies (1) The latest data for the United States, the United Kingdom and the euro area are for January 2022, while those for the others are for December 2021. (2) “Advanced Asian economies” include Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong and Singapore. (3) “Emerging Asian economies” include Mainland China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook is subject to significant uncertainties, with risks tilted to the downside, and will depend on the evolution of the pandemic and related supply-chain disruptions, how the impact of geopolitical tensions on global trade, inflation and financial market sentiment develops, and the policy responses of major central banks to inflation. Regarding the pandemic, most governments have so far responded to the recent surge in Omicron cases with targeted measures focusing on restricting high-risk activities, encouraging remote working and promoting vaccination. Compared with previous lockdown policies, these less stringent measures should help reduce supply-chain disruptions, which have shown tentative signs of improvement since late 2021 (Chart 2.3). However, in the event of a large-scale outbreak, the reimposition of lockdown measures cannot be ruled out, which could in turn lead to a renewed deterioration in supply bottlenecks. Chart 2.3 Purchasing Managers’ Index – supplier delivery times sub-index If the pandemic remains under control, supply bottlenecks are expected to ease gradually, providing some relief from goods inflation. However, several developments could cause the current high level of global inflation to persist longer than expected, including the risk that the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine and sanctions on energy imported from Russia will push up commodity prices, the delayed pass-through of higher production costs to final selling prices, the possibility that the earlier sharp rise in global residential property prices will drive up rents subsequently, upside risks to wage growth from tight labour markets, and rising inflation expectations. In particular, given that US inflation recorded its largest increase in decades, the US Federal Reserve shifted to a more hawkish policy stance at the December 2021 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, no longer characterising high inflation as “transitory” and doubling the pace of asset purchase reductions from US$15 billion per month to US$30 billion, with a view to ending the asset purchase programme by March 2022, while beginning discussions on reducing its balance sheet. Indeed, recent market pricing indicated that the US Federal Reserve might raise interest rates several times in 2022. By contrast, given the euro area’s closer trade and financial links with Russia and Ukraine, the European Central Bank may face more significant policy trade-offs. Against this background, and with global debt levels and asset valuations remaining elevated after a prolonged period of accommodative policies, if persistent inflationary pressures require the US Federal Reserve to tighten policy faster than expected, borrowers’ debt-servicing capacity could be at risk of deterioration and financial market volatility could be triggered. More recently, as geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe intensified, risk aversion in financial markets increased and signs of US dollar shortages emerged, including a widening of cross-currency swap spreads. In the event of premature tightening of global financial conditions, emerging market economies with weaker fundamentals and still affected by the pandemic may be vulnerable to renewed growth slowdowns, currency depreciation and capital outflow pressures. Increased market volatility could also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risks. Box 1 discusses whether swing pricing, a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds, can reduce the liquidity risks of these funds during periods of market stress, as well as the tool’s potential limitations. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, although the spread of the Delta variant weakened growth momentum in the third quarter, particularly in some Southeast Asian economies (Chart 2.4). Meanwhile, as major technology-product-exporting economies in the region, South Korea and Singapore continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products, further widening the unevenness of the recovery across the region. In addition, inflationary pressures remained moderate in several emerging Asian economies. Chart 2.4 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index Emerging Asian markets are generally expected to see a broad-based recovery in 2022, but the region’s near-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, although the Omicron variant has spread across the region since the end of 2021, its economic impact has so far been milder than that of previous waves of infections. Nevertheless, some economies in the region where vaccination rates still lag and public health resources are relatively constrained will continue to face the threat of new variants. Second, US Federal Reserve policy normalisation may trigger capital outflows and exert depreciation pressure on regional currencies. Economies in the region that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policies to support the economic recovery will face more difficult trade-offs between containing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity. At the long end of the yield curve, the risk of a sudden surge in long-term US yields could also spill over to long-term bond yields in emerging Asia, given their historically high correlation (Chart 2.5), increasing the risk of corrections in regional asset markets. Chart 2.5 Correlation between Asian ten-year sovereign bond yields and corresponding US Treasury yields Third, the region’s merchandise trade outlook faces uncertainties arising from the slowdown in major economies and a possible shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, which may weaken the region’s export growth. Chart 2.6 United States: imports from emerging Asia and real gross domestic product Fourth, although the region’s economies have relatively limited trade and financial links with Russia and Ukraine, the increase in commodity prices caused by the conflict will feed through to regional inflation while weakening consumption. Together with increased global economic uncertainty, this will make monetary policy normalisation decisions more complicated for regional central banks. Central banks in some economies in the region with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. The pandemic has also alerted the region’s economies to the long-term need to rebuild more sustainable and resilient growth models in preparation for other risks such as climate change. To this end, investors need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 examines whether stock market returns are affected by changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is affected by companies’ environmental performance. The coronavirus pandemic caused an enormous shock to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turmoil, some open-ended funds experienced substantial outflows (Chart B1.1), placing pressure on their liquidity management. Chart B1.1 Outflows from some open-ended funds during the March 2020 episode Apart from investors’ liquidity needs, another reason for the substantial outflows may have been investors exercising a “first-mover advantage” by redeeming their fund holdings early, thereby avoiding redemption costs that could surge during periods of market stress. To curb outflows caused by the first-mover advantage, some open-ended funds adopt swing pricing, an open-ended fund pricing rule that reduces investors’ first-mover advantage. Although many open-ended funds used swing pricing during this episode, no empirical research had established whether swing pricing could effectively reduce outflows from open-ended funds. Against this background, this box conducts an empirical study to determine whether swing pricing reduced outflows from open-ended funds during the March 2020 episode, thereby lowering their liquidity risks. In addition, this box identifies factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during periods of market stress. Based on these assessments, we put forward policy recommendations from a financial stability perspective. First-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming ahead of other investors, thereby passing redemption costs on to them. First-mover advantage mainly exists in open-ended funds that use traditional pricing rules, under which the subscription and redemption costs of fund investors, such as transaction costs arising from portfolio adjustments, are reflected in the prices of open-ended funds after transactions take place. Under this pricing mechanism, investors who redeem their shares first do not have to bear such transaction costs. This gives them an incentive to redeem their fund holdings early, particularly when substantial redemption costs are expected. Therefore, during periods of market stress, first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced because redemption costs are expected to rise. This magnifies the redemption pressures and liquidity risks faced by open-ended funds.

With goods exports and private consumption continuing to grow, the Hong Kong economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, returning to positive full-year growth for the first time since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local infections and the resulting tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on local economic activity. The overall economy is expected to sustain its recovery in 2022 as a whole, although the strength and pace of the recovery will be affected by uncertainties and risks such as the pandemic and US monetary policy normalisation. These headwinds may also affect the labour market outlook following its notable improvement in 2021. Although local inflation may edge up in the near term as import prices rise, subdued local rents and labour costs should contain overall price pressures. The Hong Kong economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021. On a year-on-year basis, real gross domestic product grew further by 5.5% in the third quarter and by 4.8% in the fourth quarter (Table 3.A), although the pace of growth slowed from the first half of the year. For 2021 as a whole, real gross domestic product grew by 6.4%, marking the first full year of positive growth since 2019. Chart 3.1 Real gross domestic product growth and contributions from major expenditure components On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity grew moderately by 0.6% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively (Chart 3.1). On the domestic front, improving labour market conditions, together with the Government’s Consumption Voucher Scheme, boosted private consumption. However, overall investment expenditure declined in the final quarter after rebounding strongly for two consecutive quarters. On the external front, as the global economy continued to recover, Hong Kong’s merchandise trade remained robust, while trade in services stayed weak, partly because inbound tourism remained at a standstill (Chart 3.2). In net terms, external trade was a drag on gross domestic product in the third quarter, but supported gross domestic product growth in the fourth quarter. Chart 3.2 Export and import volumes A new wave of local infections and the resulting tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on local economic activity in early 2022. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional countercyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the 100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme and various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme will be enhanced, with higher maximum loan amounts and extended application and repayment periods. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, has also extended the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to end-October 2022. The Scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year partial principal repayment option, which is also applicable to loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. The Hong Kong economy is expected to continue recovering in 2022 as a whole, but at a slower pace than in 2021, partly reflecting slower global economic growth amid the ongoing pandemic and a higher base effect. In particular, Hong Kong’s goods exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The Government’s implementation of various capital works and infrastructure projects will also support the economy. The Government forecasts real gross domestic product growth of between 2.0% and 3.5% in 2022, while the growth forecasts of international organisations and private-sector analysts average 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of Hong Kong’s economic recovery are subject to the numerous uncertainties and risks discussed in the preceding chapters. In particular, recent pandemic developments, the faster pace of US monetary policy normalisation, and heightened geopolitical concerns (such as the Russia-Ukraine situation) have clouded the near-term economic outlook for Hong Kong and the world. On the other hand, an earlier-than-expected resumption of quarantine-free travel between Hong Kong and Mainland China could stimulate local economic growth. As the economy recovered, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% at year-end (Chart 3.3). Total employment in December 2021 also rebounded by 2.0% from the recent trough in February 2021, but remained below its pre-pandemic level. In early 2022, official data showed that labour market pressures re-emerged amid a new wave of local infections. In addition, a decline in the number of online job advertisements also indicated fewer new vacancies. Looking ahead, the new wave of local infections and the tightening of anti-epidemic measures will put some pressure on the local labour market in the near term, particularly in sectors involving face-to-face contact. Over the longer term, labour market conditions will depend on local pandemic developments and the pace of the local economic recovery. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Local inflationary pressures have generally increased in recent months, but have remained moderate. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying consumer price inflation rate edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022 (Chart 3.4). The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also picked up in recent months. In particular, as local demand recovered and external prices rose (Chart 3.5), prices for meals out and some energy-related items increased at a faster pace. Meanwhile, the private housing rent component of the Composite Consumer Price Index continued to decline broadly, thereby containing overall inflation momentum (Chart 3.6). Although real unit labour costs remained subdued, they rose slightly in recent quarters, partly due to an improvement in real average salaries (Chart 3.7). Chart 3.4 Different indicators of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Hong Kong import prices Chart 3.6 Rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index and market rents Chart 3.7 Unit labour costs Looking ahead, local inflation is expected to edge up in the near term amid rising import prices and pandemic-induced logistics disruptions. However, subdued rents and moderate local labour cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. The market consensus forecasts the headline inflation rate to reach 2.4% in 2022, while the Government forecasts a headline inflation rate of 2.1% and an underlying inflation rate of 2.0% for 2022.

Amid risk-off sentiment in the local stock market and concerns over the normalisation of US monetary policy, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened during the review period. Given ample Hong Kong dollar liquidity, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates continued to remain low. Overall, trading in the Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and money markets continued to be smooth and orderly. Looking ahead, although uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, the pandemic and escalating geopolitical tensions may intensify capital flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, enabling it to withstand shocks arising from capital flow volatility. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar stayed on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone most of the time, and trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar had gradually weakened against the US dollar amid risk-off sentiment in the local stock market (Chart 4.1). Although the Hong Kong dollar rebounded slightly in October 2021 as market sentiment improved, its appreciation subsequently lost momentum, mainly due to weak southbound net buying through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.2), as well as market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen as the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy outlook turned more hawkish. During the review period, initial public offering activities continued to support the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.3). Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no notable signs of funds flowing out of the local banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments figures showed that non-residents’ direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the second half of 2021, with no signs of unusual cross-border fund flows. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Southbound net buying through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect Chart 4.3 Equity funds raised on the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX) Despite the strengthening of the US dollar during the review period, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index remained stable because of the renminbi’s appreciation against the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.4). Given the very small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index broadly tracked the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.4 Nominal and real effective exchange rates Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, pandemic developments and escalating geopolitical tensions may intensify capital flow volatility. As US dollar interest rates rise, under the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS), outflows of Hong Kong dollar funds, the pace and scale of which will depend on prevailing market conditions, may weaken the Hong Kong dollar and trigger the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking. Hong Kong also has ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, enabling it to withstand capital flow volatility without compromising financial stability. During the review period, monetary conditions in Hong Kong remained accommodative. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base increased by 1.4% over the eight months since end-June 2021, mainly driven by an increase in Certificates of Indebtedness. Reflecting additional issuance to meet banks’ continued demand for Exchange Fund Bills amid ample liquidity in the banking system, Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased by HK$119.7 billion to HK$1,188.7 billion during the review period, while the Aggregate Balance (before Discount Window activities) decreased correspondingly by HK$119.9 billion to HK$337.6 billion (Chart 4.5). Meanwhile, government-issued notes and coins remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes Over the six months since end-July 2021, total deposits with authorised institutions grew moderately by 4.5%, while Hong Kong dollar deposits edged up by 0.3%. It should, however, be noted that monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various short-term factors, such as seasonal and initial public offering-related funding demand, as well as business- and investment-related activities, and it is therefore appropriate to observe longer-term trends. For 2021 as a whole, total deposits and Hong Kong dollar deposits increased by 4.6% and 1.4% respectively. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorised institutions by currency Overall, trading in Hong Kong’s interbank market continued to be smooth and orderly. Given ample liquidity in the banking system, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates remained low despite market concerns over US monetary tightening (Chart 4.7). Partly reflecting market expectations of increased funding demand towards year-end, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates edged up in December 2021. The average lending rate for new mortgages increased slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. Meanwhile, the best lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Looking ahead, ample liquidity in the banking system will provide an adequate buffer in the event of large-scale capital market activities or financial market volatility. Chart 4.7 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank offered rates During the review period, the offshore renminbi interbank market continued to operate normally. Affected by seasonal liquidity demand towards year-end, the overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate experienced slight fluctuations in late December 2021, while the 3-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate remained relatively stable and hovered around 3% throughout the review period (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Overnight and 3-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate fixings In the second half of 2021, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to grow steadily. Over the six months since end-July 2021, outstanding renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased by 30.3% to RMB1,113.5 billion at end-January 2022 (Chart 4.9 and Table 4.A). Of these, renminbi customer deposits increased by 33.5%, mainly driven by inflows of corporate funds, offsetting a 48.0% decline in outstanding certificates of deposit. Chart 4.9 Renminbi deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong During the six-month period since July 2021, although outstanding renminbi loans decreased by 10.2% to RMB167.6 billion, renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow. Between end-July 2021 and end-January 2022, transactions handled by local banks reached RMB3,763.0 billion (Chart 4.10), an increase of 18.3% from RMB3,181.0 billion in the same period a year earlier. Hong Kong’s sizeable renminbi liquidity pool continued to support a large volume of renminbi payment and financing transactions. For 2021 as a whole, the average daily turnover of the Renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system increased from RMB1,191.5 billion in 2020 to RMB1,522.6 billion. Chart 4.10 Renminbi trade settlement remittances Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the establishment of the two-way northbound and southbound Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Bond Connect and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect, the continued opening of the Mainland’s capital account, growing international investor demand for renminbi assets, and deeper regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives. Major global stock markets continued to advance in the fourth quarter of 2021, but consolidated from January 2022 amid growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict. The Hong Kong stock market remained sluggish in the fourth quarter of 2021, mainly dragged down by a sharp decline in technology stocks. Global risks and uncertainty over pandemic developments in Hong Kong caused the Hang Seng Index to fall to a nearly two-year low at the end of February. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi bond market continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. The residential property market had softened since mid-2021, partly affected by weaker asset market sentiment and a new wave of the local pandemic. Major global stock markets generally continued to advance in the final quarter of 2021, taking the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on 4 January 2022 (Chart 4.11). Stimulative government monetary and fiscal policies, the global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings supported the rally in major global stock markets, although the pandemic remained investors’ principal risk concern throughout the year. However, major global stock markets consolidated from early January 2022 amid growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies in the face of sharply rising inflation risks, surging commodity prices, and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict. By comparison, the Hong Kong stock market continued to lag behind other major global stock markets at the end of 2021. The Hang Seng Index hovered between 24,000 and 26,500 points from September to mid-November and closed at 23,398 points at end-2021, down 14.1% from 2020. In early 2022, buying interest from value investors returned to the Hong Kong stock market, driving the Hang Seng Index back to around 25,000 points in January. However, uncertainty over pandemic developments in Hong Kong and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict dragged the Hang Seng Index down to a nearly two-year low of 22,713 points at the end of February. Over the entire review period from end-August 2021 to February 2022, the Hang Seng Index fell by 12.2%, while the MSCI World Index declined by 5.2% (Chart 4.11). Chart 4.11 Hang Seng Index and MSCI World Index Owing to the emergence of the highly transmissible Omicron variant, equity market implied volatility fluctuated sharply at the end of November 2021 before subsequently receding. Although the skew index retreated from its record high in late June 2021, it remained elevated, reflecting investor concerns over a correction in the prolonged equity market rebound since the outbreak of the pandemic and their willingness to commit more funds to hedge against downside equity market risks (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12 Option-implied volatility of the Hang Seng Index and S&P 500 Index, and the skew index Against the backdrop of ample global liquidity, Hong Kong stocks continued to record net inflows from international investors since the previous report (Chart 4.13). By comparison, southbound trading under Stock Connect recorded substantial net outflows in the third quarter of 2021, mainly due to concerns over the impact of changes in Mainland regulation on technology stocks. However, buying through southbound Stock Connect began to recover in December 2021, with total inflows of HK$98.3 billion by the end of February. During the review period, cumulative net buying increased by 5.7% to HK$2,233.0 billion (Chart 4.14). Chart 4.13 Net fund inflows into Hong Kong’s stock market Chart 4.14 Net flows through Stock Connect schemes After funds raised in Hong Kong’s primary market reached a record high in the first half of 2021, activity slowed in the second half. There were 98 initial public offerings in 2021 as a whole, raising a total of HK$328.9 billion (Chart 4.15), with total funds raised down 17.8% from the previous year. In 2021, HKEX ranked fourth in the global initial public offering market, behind only Nasdaq, the New York Stock Exchange and the Shanghai Stock Exchange. Chart 4.15 Hong Kong’s initial public offering market The outlook for the local stock market remains uncertain. Monetary policy easing in the Mainland and more US-listed Chinese companies pursuing secondary listings in Hong Kong’s primary market will improve sentiment in the Hong Kong stock market. However, the stock market still faces many headwinds, including uncertainty over local pandemic developments, a faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalisation, and an escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

The profitability of Hong Kong retail banks declined in the second half of 2021. The classified loan ratio edged up in the second half of 2021, but remained low by both historical and international standards. With robust capital and liquidity positions, the Hong Kong banking sector remained sound. During the review period, the HKMA extended a number of support measures to further help the economy weather the difficult period. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may threaten the economic recovery, while the risk of a faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalisation will also pose challenges to banks’ credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of the relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. In the second half of 2021, retail banks’ aggregate pre-tax operating profit fell by 16.1% from the same period in 2020. The weak profit performance was mainly attributable to decreases in net interest and non-interest income and an increase in operating expenses. Consequently, the return on assets declined to 0.50% in the second half of 2021, compared with 0.61% in the same period in 2020 (Chart 5.1). For 2021 as a whole, retail banks’ aggregate pre-tax operating profit decreased by 18.6% from 2020, while the return on assets declined from 0.77% to 0.59%. Chart 5.1 Retail bank profitability Reflecting the continued impact of the low interest rate environment, retail banks’ net interest margin also remained at a low level of 0.98% in the second half of 2021 (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Retail banks’ net interest margin Reflecting year-end funding demand and the decline in the Aggregate Balance following the HKMA’s additional issuance of Exchange Fund Bills, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate recorded a slight increase in the final quarter of 2021. However, as banking system liquidity remained very ample, interbank rates continued to stay at low levels. Specifically, the 3-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate edged up by 9 basis points from six months earlier to 0.26% at end-December 2021 (the blue line in Chart 5.3). Retail banks’ funding costs remained stable during the review period. In particular, the composite interest rate, a measure of retail banks’ average cost of Hong Kong dollar funding, rose modestly by 3 basis points from 0.18% six months earlier to 0.21% at end-2021 (the green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Period averages for newly approved loans. (c) Since June 2019, the composite interest rate has been calculated under the newly implemented local “interest rate risk in the banking book” framework. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards are not strictly comparable with those for earlier months. From a broader perspective, the aggregate Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of locally licensed banks edged up by 6 basis points in the second half of 2021 (the red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks Since June 2019, all licensed banks subject to the new local interest rate risk in the banking book framework have submitted returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks have continued to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. The aggregate funding cost has been calculated as the weighted average of the relevant figures for these two categories of licensed banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards are not directly comparable with those for earlier months. Although US monetary policy normalisation may signal an improvement in banks’ profitability, the near-term improvement may be partly offset by two factors. First, despite the Federal Reserve’s indication that it would raise interest rates several times in 2022, past experience suggests that changes in local interest rates may lag behind those in the US, particularly when liquidity in Hong Kong’s interbank market remains very ample. Therefore, it may take more time for improvements in banks’ net interest margins to materialise. In addition, the surge in Omicron variant cases may create uncertainty over the pace of economic recovery, thereby putting pressure on banks’ asset quality and profitability. Climate change affects every aspect of life, and everyone has a responsibility to help mitigate its impact. In this regard, the HKMA has devoted substantial efforts to advancing Hong Kong’s climate goals and contributing to global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following the inclusion of our first Sustainability Report as a chapter in the HKMA Annual Report 2021 last year, we are publishing the Sustainability Report 2022 separately for the first time this year. I hope this report will give readers a deeper understanding of the HKMA’s strategies and priorities in strengthening the resilience of Hong Kong’s banking system to climate change, developing a green finance ecosystem, and fulfilling our roles as a responsible investor and a sustainable organisation. During the year, we made significant progress in advancing sustainability across the HKMA’s key functions. Details of our initiatives and work are set out in this report, with the following highlights: Banks’ day-to-day operations are exposed to climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA has taken concrete steps to strengthen banks’ climate resilience. In 2022, we formulated a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into our supervisory processes and explored how technology could be used to help banks assess the impact of physical risks. In view of the growing number of green and sustainable products launched by banks, we also shared with the industry good practices for the proper management of these products, with a view to enhancing banks’ climate risk management capabilities. The HKMA actively participates in collaborative initiatives to address climate risks and promote the development of sustainable finance. Locally, we are working with other financial regulators through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group) to develop a local green classification framework, which will enhance financial market transparency and improve the consistency of green finance policies. Internationally, we participate actively in various international organisations to help formulate policies for addressing climate change and assess its impact on financial stability. Hong Kong is well positioned to meet Asia’s demand for green and sustainable financing. Although 2022 was a particularly challenging year for global bond markets, green and sustainable debt issuance in Hong Kong continued to record strong growth, rising by 42% to US$80.5 billion in total, making Hong Kong Asia’s largest hub for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances². The issuers included the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government and the Hainan Provincial People’s Government, whose issuances once again demonstrated Hong Kong’s unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the Mainland and international markets. The vibrant development of Hong Kong’s green bond market is partly attributable to the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the Government in issuing green bonds totalling nearly US$16 billion, with the proceeds allocated to more than 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and conservation. We also helped the Government achieve two “firsts”, including assisting it in issuing the first batch of government green retail bonds totalling HK$20 billion in May 2022, which was the world’s largest green retail bond issuance at the time. We also assisted the Government in issuing the first batch of tokenised green bonds in February 2023. These were among the world’s first tokenised green bonds issued by a government, and the issuance also marked a milestone in our successful integration of Hong Kong’s strengths in the bond market, green and sustainable finance, and financial technology. Standards, data and talent are indispensable to the sound development of the climate finance ecosystem, and can only be established through the efforts and collaboration of different sectors. To this end, the HKMA works mainly through the Steering Group with relevant government departments, regulators, academic institutions and the financial industry to develop these elements. In addition to developing the local green classification framework mentioned above, the Steering Group also promotes skills training in the industry and enhances Hong Kong’s data resources through its Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance. The Steering Group has also made good progress in other areas, including mandatory climate-related disclosures and carbon market opportunities. In 2022, the HKMA further strengthened the Exchange Fund’s responsible investment efforts, notably by setting a target of achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions for the Exchange Fund’s investment portfolio by 2050. At the same time, we enhanced risk management to improve the Exchange Fund’s climate resilience and risk-adjusted long-term returns. In addition, to fully capture the potential opportunities arising from climate change, we are committed to promoting sustainable investment by the Exchange Fund and identifying investment opportunities that support climate transition and climate change mitigation, thereby enhancing the portfolio’s long-term returns. At the end of 2021, the weighted average carbon intensity of the Exchange Fund’s equity portfolio was 43% lower than its 2017 level. In fact, the Exchange Fund’s exposure to carbon-intensive assets has consistently remained below that of the broader market. Going forward, we will continue progressing towards the net-zero target by further integrating environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management process, exercising active ownership, maintaining ongoing collaboration with stakeholders, and focusing on portfolio decarbonisation and transition. At the HKMA, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee, which I chair, is responsible for formulating the HKMA’s sustainability strategy. Our strategic direction is based on three pillars: the environment, our people and social responsibility. On the environment, we are committed to promoting a green workplace and more environmentally friendly markets among the public. On our people, as a responsible and caring employer, we actively foster a healthy and inclusive workplace. On social responsibility, we strive to enhance the public’s financial literacy, promote financial inclusion and actively give back to the community. Compared with the levels in 2015, when we began tracking our carbon footprint, our per capita greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption and paper use all recorded double-digit reductions in 2022. More importantly, we have developed a roadmap for achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. In the short term, our targets are to eliminate Scope 1 emissions entirely and, using 2015 as the baseline, reduce Scope 2 emissions by 63% by 2030. Addressing climate change and promoting sustainable development require sustained efforts and collaboration by multiple parties. On this important global issue, we recognise that we must take concrete action, lead by example, and work with like-minded peers and international organisations. The next section outlines the HKMA’s short-term plans and priorities for addressing climate change across its key functions. Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier is a formidable task, and we will spare no effort in pursuing this target. We are confident that, through the collective efforts of all our colleagues, the financial industry and the wider community, we can successfully meet the climate challenges ahead. Chief Executive Eddie Yue

In 2023, the HKMA will continue to promote the sustainable development of Hong Kong’s financial sector and fulfil its responsibilities as a responsible investor and sustainable organisation. At the same time, through participation in international and regional organisations, the HKMA will also strive to promote the broad development of green and sustainable finance and best practices. As the banking regulator, we will strive to strengthen the banking sector’s climate resilience and further enhance our green finance ecosystem to support banks’ green transition. Specifically, the HKMA will engage with banks to understand their progress in implementing the supervisory requirements on climate risk management, incorporate climate considerations into our supervisory review process, and revise the common assessment framework for the banking sector’s “Green and Sustainable Banking Baseline”. Meanwhile, the HKMA will support banks’ efforts to enhance their climate resilience and risk management capabilities, such as exploring various measures and technological solutions to help banks identify, measure and monitor their climate risk exposures. The HKMA will also work with banks to conduct the next round of climate risk stress tests as part of the regular regulator-led stress testing exercise for 2023 to 2024. Participating banks will be required to assess their ability to withstand climate risks under an enhanced stress testing framework covering a range of stress scenarios, including extreme climate events and adverse economic conditions. To promote the sound development of banks’ provision of green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will keep abreast of local and international market and regulatory developments, maintain communication with the industry, and provide guidance on sales processes where appropriate. We will also conduct off-site thematic assessments to gain a comprehensive understanding of the green and sustainable investment products offered by banks. Meanwhile, to further develop the green finance ecosystem in support of the financial sector’s green transition, the HKMA is planning to consult the industry on the structure and core elements of a local green classification framework. On market development, to reinforce Hong Kong’s position as a regional green and sustainable finance hub, the HKMA will assist the Government in increasing the issuance of green bonds under the “Government Green Bond Programme” and broadening the programme’s scope to cover sustainable development bonds, while attracting more green financing activities to Hong Kong through the “Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme”. The HKMA will also assist in implementing the Government-funded “Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme” to expand Hong Kong’s green finance talent pool. In addition, the HKMA will continue to encourage more Mainland local governments, institutions and enterprises to conduct green financing through Hong Kong, and explore the feasibility of integrating green finance with technology. Separately, through the “Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group”, we will continue to collaborate with other authorities and departments on cross-sector issues such as skills training and data, green taxonomies, climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, as well as carbon market opportunities. Through the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks, the HKMA will jointly launch various dedicated programmes in Asia with the International Finance Corporation, including conducting green finance research, providing unique market insights, offering targeted professional training to banks, and providing practical guidance to help banks formulate roadmaps for developing green finance into a core business. Looking ahead, the Alliance will work closely with its cornerstone members, global partners and knowledge partners to launch a membership programme and expand its influence in Asia. The Alliance will also further enhance the professional capabilities of industry practitioners, facilitate green finance knowledge sharing, and lead programmes in new areas. As a responsible investor, the HKMA has set a target of achieving net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund’s investment portfolio by 2050 or earlier, as part of its commitment to global climate action and implementation of the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. Looking ahead, the HKMA will continue to incorporate environmental, social and governance factors into its investment management process, advance towards its net-zero emissions target, and fully support global climate action. As a responsible and sustainable organisation, the HKMA cares for its employees as well as the wider community and the surrounding environment. We have formulated a sustainability roadmap and set climate targets for our own operations as part of our commitment to global carbon reduction and climate action. The HKMA will continue to prioritise carbon emissions reduction and encourage employees to give their full support by conserving energy and reducing waste. In addition, we will provide employees with further guidance on incorporating sustainability principles into the procurement process. To implement digital transformation and enhance operational agility, the HKMA will explore ways to modernise its internal systems and applications, further improve operational efficiency, and minimise, as far as possible, potential risks that may arise during the digital transformation process.

Climate change is a significant risk facing the financial system. The HKMA has been committed to strengthening Hong Kong’s financial system to build a greener and more sustainable future, contributing to Hong Kong’s climate goals and the global sustainable development agenda. Banks face the impacts of various sustainability- and climate-related issues in their day-to-day business operations. To continue performing their important functions in the financial system and channel more capital towards green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA places particular emphasis on building banks’ capabilities to respond to and manage climate risks, and accelerating their efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economic model. The HKMA also supports banks in enhancing their capabilities to detect environmental crimes, and participated in the recently published Hong Kong Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment, which covers areas such as environmental crimes and illegal wildlife trafficking. In 2022, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (Basel Committee)1 published principles for the effective management and supervision of climate-related financial risks and responded to frequently asked questions to clarify how the existing Basel Framework addresses these risks. In light of these international developments, the HKMA will continue its efforts to incorporate climate-related factors into the supervisory framework. Following the issuance of the Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1 “Climate Risk Management” in 2021, the HKMA has also maintained communication with banks to exchange views on the expectations, progress and challenges relating to the implementation of the relevant supervisory requirements. To further strengthen the supervision of banks’ climate risk management, the HKMA has formulated a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into the banking supervisory process and communicated it to the banking industry in June. As part of the implementation of the two-year plan, the HKMA issued the revised Supervisory Policy Manual module SA-1 “Risk-based Supervisory Approach” and enhanced the CAMEL2 rating system by incorporating climate risk into the risk-based supervisory process. Meanwhile, drawing on the experience gained from the 2021 pilot exercise, the HKMA refined the climate risk stress-testing scenarios and assessment framework. The HKMA also formulated a plan to incorporate the next round of climate risk stress testing into regular supervisor-led stress tests, thereby enabling a more comprehensive assessment of the banking sector’s resilience under extreme climate scenarios. Under the two-year plan, the HKMA is also enhancing its green assessment framework for banks to reflect the latest developments in sustainability-related issues, including climate risk management and transition planning. Meanwhile, the HKMA is reviewing the supervisory review process used to assess and monitor banks’ capital adequacy and determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, with the aim of encouraging banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks to address risks associated with climate change and the transition to carbon neutrality. Given the growing prevalence of banks issuing green and sustainable products, the HKMA conducted a round of thematic reviews focusing primarily on banks’ development and ongoing management of these products. The HKMA identified a number of sound practices during the thematic reviews and shared them with the industry in a circular issued in December, enabling banks to progressively strengthen their climate risk management capabilities. The application of technology can improve data availability and enhance banks’ ability to manage climate risks. The HKMA has begun developing a common platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risks on real estate. In addition, the HKMA, together with other central banks and regulators, completed a project under the BIS Innovation Hub to explore how technological solutions could facilitate physical risk assessments. The HKMA also attaches great importance to promoting sustainable and globally leading anti-money laundering practices; this work employs advanced analytics and compliance technology, complemented by fully automated regulatory data collection. Over the past 12 months, the HKMA has streamlined the collection process for anti-money laundering supervisory data to reduce banks’ manual workload and paper consumption. To enhance transparency across financial markets and improve the consistency of green finance policies, the HKMA collaborated with other financial regulators to establish a local green classification framework. A green classification framework, commonly known as a green taxonomy, classifies economic activities as green or sustainable, providing a reference for authorities and market participants to determine whether an activity or its related products are genuinely green or sustainable. To this end, the HKMA has maintained engagement with the industry and other relevant stakeholders to explore the framework’s features and challenges in depth, and is preparing to make recommendations and conduct a consultation on the framework’s structure and core elements in the first half of 2023. Recognising that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system, the HKMA has incorporated a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into its financial risk analysis and research to strengthen its current surveillance work. The HKMA takes climate change into account in its ongoing monitoring of financial stability risks and includes analyses of climate-related risks in its financial stability reports. Through active participation in the Scenario Design and Analysis workstream under the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA helped further enrich climate scenarios, enabling central banks and regulators to gain a clearer understanding of the macroeconomic and financial impacts of climate change. In terms of research, the HKMA conducted several applied research projects in 2022 to examine in depth two major topics, namely greenwashing in the corporate green bond market3 and the role of disclosure in mitigating climate risk exposures4. The findings of these studies help inform the formulation of policies and supervisory measures to address the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Locally, these studies help strengthen the HKMA’s ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Externally, the HKMA has shared its research findings with a broad range of stakeholders through various channels, including international central bank research conferences and its Half-Yearly Monetary and Financial Stability Report. The HKMA’s “Liquidity Facilities Framework” is a collateralised standby funding arrangement that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. The HKMA is studying the incorporation of sustainability considerations into the assessment of eligible collateral under this framework. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risks and mainstreaming sustainable finance. Through such participation, the HKMA helps foster international and regional policy dialogue on addressing climate change and its impact on financial stability, while drawing insights from it to strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong’s financial system.

To consolidate Hong Kong’s position as a regional green and sustainable finance hub, the HKMA stepped up its efforts to enhance market awareness and participation, provide the necessary infrastructure and enablers, and support international initiatives to align with global standards. The Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), co-chaired by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), is responsible for coordinating the financial sector’s response to climate and environmental risks, accelerating the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supporting the Government’s climate strategies1. The Steering Group’s work is primarily guided by its Strategic Plan, which sets out 6 key long-term focus areas and 5 key near-term action points to strengthen Hong Kong’s financial ecosystem for a greener and more sustainable future (Figure 1). Strengthen climate-related financial risk management to consolidate Hong Kong’s position as a global risk management centre; promote the flow of climate-related information at all levels to facilitate risk management, capital allocation and investor protection; enhance relevant skills among practitioners and raise public awareness and understanding; encourage product innovation and research initiatives to direct capital towards green and sustainable projects; capitalise on opportunities presented by the Mainland to develop Hong Kong into a green finance centre for the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (Greater Bay Area); and strengthen regional and international collaboration. Actions taken to date to advance sustainable finance development in Hong Kong: The Steering Group has made good progress since its establishment. Its current priorities include skills training and data collection under the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance (see below), a green classification catalogue (see “Developing a green classification framework to facilitate green finance” in the chapter “Building a Sustainable Financial System” on page 9), climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. In particular, the Steering Group announced in March the preliminary feasibility assessment of carbon market opportunities for Hong Kong, and will support Hong Kong’s development into a regional carbon trading centre, including by developing a high-quality international voluntary carbon market and capitalising on opportunities arising from Greater Bay Area collaboration. In December, the Steering Group announced its collaboration with CDP2 to enhance data availability and strengthen sustainability reporting in Hong Kong. As part of the collaboration, the two parties developed a climate and environmental risk questionnaire for non-listed companies and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which not only facilitates sustainability reporting by companies, but also assists financial institutions in collecting and analysing company-level data for risk assessment and related business decisions. This marks an important step in broadening the coverage of the Steering Group’s data work to include SMEs, an important segment of the economy that has traditionally been more difficult to reach. The Steering Group established the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance in July 2021 to coordinate the efforts of financial regulators, government bureaux and departments, industry stakeholders and academia in training and policy development, and to establish resource and data repositories. In the first half of 2022, the Centre launched 3 repositories covering data, training information and internship opportunities respectively, helping the financial sector and other sectors access data and learning resources related to green and sustainable finance. The repository provides data sources for assessing physical risks in Hong Kong. To support industry talent development, the Centre assisted the Government in launching the “Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme” in December, providing subsidies to practitioners, students and graduates participating in green and sustainable finance-related training and skills enhancement. Other initiatives to promote skills training included launching the “Sustainable Finance Internship Initiative” to create more internship opportunities for students, and developing a new “Green and Sustainable Finance” module3 under the HKMA’s “Enhanced Competency Framework” for banking practitioners. “Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme” The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance in the region. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA launched the “Alliance for Green Commercial Banks”4, bringing together regional financial institutions, banking industry associations, research institutions and innovative technology providers to develop a collaborative platform for green commercial banking. The Alliance aims to enable commercial banks and other financial institutions to realise their full potential in making green finance a mainstream core business, and to promote the financial system’s participation in global climate change-related activities. Operating model: provide financial institutions with a one-stop mutual learning platform to access the knowledge, tools and information needed to formulate their own green finance roadmaps and transform themselves into credible green financial institutions; bring together green finance leaders, connect green financial institutions across different emerging markets, facilitate communication and explore frontier topics; advance the global green finance agenda and unlock boundless green and climate-related investment opportunities. In June, 5 leading global financial institutions5 became cornerstone members of the Alliance and worked closely with the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA to encourage clients to adopt green strategies, promote best practices for green products and services, and unlock new business opportunities, thereby supporting the transition to a green economy. In addition, 3 global partners and 1 knowledge partner6 committed in 2022 to providing climate expertise in areas ranging from innovation and standardisation to academic research. Details of the Alliance and its membership structure are available on the relevant webpage (English version): Cornerstone members, the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA sign a Memorandum of Understanding. Separately, since March 2021, the Alliance has held a total of 18 training events and roundtable discussions, attracting more than 6,000 participants from around the world, including the Asia-Pacific region, Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Americas. In addition, in June 2022, the Alliance and the Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research (HKIMR)7 jointly published their first frontier topic research report, entitled “Climate Risk: Definitions, Measurement, Current Practices and Regulatory Oversight”. The HKMA has continued to promote green and sustainable debt issuance and foster a local ecosystem of related professional services. Total green and sustainable debt issued in Hong Kong in 2022, including bonds and loans, reached US$80.5 billion, an increase of 42%. +42% green and sustainable debt issuance (US$80.5 billion). To demonstrate the Government’s commitment to combating climate change, promoting green finance, and developing Hong Kong into a more sustainable and liveable city, the Government launched the “Government Green Bond Programme” in 2018, with the HKMA assisting in the issuance of the relevant green bonds. To date, the Government has issued close to US$16 billion equivalent in green institutional and retail bonds, with the proceeds allocated to more than 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and conservation. To enhance the transparency and accountability of the Programme, the Government publishes the “Green Bond Report” annually, providing details of the allocation of green bond proceeds and the expected environmental benefits. To enable members of the public to participate in and share the benefits of Hong Kong’s sustainable development through investment, the inaugural batch of green retail bonds totalling HK$20 billion was issued in May and received an enthusiastic response from the public, making it the world’s largest green retail bond issuance at the time. The issuance also broadened the range of green and sustainable financial products in Hong Kong and consolidated Hong Kong’s position as a leading green finance hub regionally and internationally. The Government also continued its regular issuance of green institutional bonds in the 2022-23 financial year and issued US$5.75 billion equivalent in green bonds in January 2023. This triple-currency issuance comprised US dollar, euro and renminbi tranches with tenors ranging from 2 to 30 years, continuing to provide important benchmarks for potential issuers in Hong Kong and the region. The issuance was well received by the global investment community and successfully attracted new investors who had not participated in the Government’s previous green bond issuances, reflecting investors’ confidence in Hong Kong’s long-term credit standing and economic fundamentals. In response to investor demand, the Government doubled the issuance size of the renminbi bonds to RMB10 billion. The shares taken up by international investors and Mainland investors participating through Bond Connect “Southbound Trading” also increased, demonstrating Hong Kong’s status as the leading offshore renminbi business hub and further consolidating its leading position as an international financial centre. In February 2023, the HKMA also assisted the Government in issuing a tokenised institutional green bond to test the use of distributed ledger technology for bond issuance and settlement. This was among the world’s first tokenised green bonds issued by a government. The primary issuance was settled on a T+1 basis over a private blockchain network, with subsequent processes, including coupon payment, secondary market trading settlement and redemption at maturity, also digitalised. The Government’s experience from this issuance can serve as a reference for market participants interested in conducting similar bond issuances in the future. To provide the industry with credible and accessible market information, the HKMA continued to collaborate with the Climate Bonds Initiative and the International Capital Market Association to publish annual reports on the green debt markets in Hong Kong and the region respectively. The International Capital Market Association’s report showed that in 2022 Hong Kong became the largest hub in Asia for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances, with bonds arranged in Hong Kong totalling US$27.8 billion, accounting for more than approximately one-third of the regional total. Asia’s largest hub for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances: US$27.8 billion. Following its inaugural issuance in 2021, the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government issued another RMB5 billion of offshore local government bonds in Hong Kong in November 2022, including RMB2.6 billion of green and blue bonds8. In the same month, the Hainan Provincial People’s Government also issued RMB5 billion of offshore bonds in Hong Kong for the first time, including blue and sustainable bonds. These bond issuances once again highlighted Hong Kong’s unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the Mainland and the rest of the world, as well as its longstanding position as the region’s premier fundraising platform. The HKMA continued to promote and implement the “Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme” launched in 2021, and leveraged the Scheme to attract more related professional service providers, including financial institutions, green advisory firms and external reviewers, to establish and expand their operations in Hong Kong. The Scheme has been well received by the industry. By the end of 2022, the Scheme had covered the external review expenses of issuers of more than 180 green and sustainable debt instruments for pre-issuance, post-issuance, or both, helping issuers ensure and demonstrate rigorous adherence to market best practices and international standards. From March, the Scheme was enhanced by lowering the minimum loan size threshold for external review expense grant applications from HK$200 million to HK$100 million, helping smaller enterprises obtain green financing. Following the successful completion of the proof-of-concept for tokenised retail green bonds under Project Genesis in 2021, the HKMA and the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre collaborated again under Genesis 2.0 to explore the technical feasibility of digitalised carbon forwards, also known as mitigation outcome interests (MOIs), with a view to enhancing the transparency, objectivity and environmental attributes of the green bond market. The project was completed in October 2022, successfully developing two prototypes that use blockchain and other related technologies to track, deliver and transfer digitalised MOIs.

As one of the world’s largest asset owners and managers, the HKMA plays an important role in promoting the development of green and sustainable finance in support of the global climate change agenda. The HKMA is also a pioneer in responsible investment. As early as 2015, it took the lead in investing in green and sustainable assets, required its external investment managers to adopt the Principles of Responsible Ownership promulgated by the Securities and Futures Commission, and incorporated environmental, social and governance factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. Investing prudently in accordance with the principle of “capital preservation first, long-term growth thereafter”, the HKMA believes that taking environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into account can unlock long-term sustainable value for investments and mitigate associated risks. In the face of mounting climate change challenges, the HKMA continues to advance its responsible investment journey, including setting a “net-zero emissions by 2050” target in 2022 and enhancing its risk management strategies to improve portfolio resilience, thereby seeking better risk-adjusted long-term returns for the Exchange Fund. The HKMA also actively participates in building the green and sustainable finance ecosystem, partnering with like-minded investors and regulators to promote responsible investment and collaborating with international organisations to formulate ESG investment standards. Transparency of climate-related information plays a pivotal role in managing climate risks. To fulfil its commitment to supporting the Glasgow Declaration issued by the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) at the 2021 United Nations Climate Change Conference and to greening the global financial system, the HKMA makes climate-related disclosures for the Exchange Fund in accordance with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) under the Financial Stability Board. a.
